He expects a big market in helping people find purpose without work and in real human connection, and says education should be rethought around being happy and building real connection with other humans, which he guesses will be the main skill.

He is skeptical that UBI is the right answer, though he admits few alternatives have been articulated. His idea is "machine money" versus "human money": machine money is what technology produces, and you want massive deflation toward zero prices. Human money is earned by pro-social acts such as coaching Little League and spent on human things like art. How to fund machine money, he jokes, is something 10x more intelligence might answer.

chunks.heading: What he'd tell startups: sell the service, hire the agile
chunks.text:
On advice to founders, Paul says the future has never been harder to predict, and things are moving faster than most people predicted 5 years ago. YC's fundamental rule still applies: back people who are really smart and agile, who keep re-evaluating and don't lock into a 5-year plan. That agility is an advantage over incumbents, who can't pivot as fast.

He says he doesn't get into sector-level detail (that is the group partners' job), but what he sees working best is startups that deliver a service rather than sell software, so customers get immediate ROI. His example: "we're going to take over your customer service." With AI tools, some YC companies reach about $10M in revenue within a year with roughly a dozen employees, which he says would not have been seen 10 years ago.

He also expects intelligence to be embedded everywhere, comparing it to microprocessors now sitting inside USB cables and power cords. He mentions talking toys, such as robotic cat toys and teddy bears that talk, as one example.

chunks.heading: Health: a CGM, ChatGPT as a second opinion, and AI plus doctors
chunks.text:
Paul is enthusiastic about AI in healthcare and wellness. The medical system mostly treats vague symptoms, and he expects deeper, more mechanistic, individualized care. He sees AI as a way to deal with doctor shortages, including in places like villages in India with no other option.

- **Personal example:** he had trouble sleeping and worked it out in a ChatGPT conversation. Too much hot yoga was overactivating his sympathetic nervous system, acting "almost like caffeine" and raising his resting heart rate. He cut back and sleeps again.
- **Hospitals are dangerous:** his first child was born about 100 days early and spent months in the NICU, with five surgeries. He learned as much as he could so he could question doctors. A resident was about to start a third course of a medication that can destroy a child's kidneys; he says medical errors are one of the leading causes of death. His father was nearly harmed by an unprescribed insulin shot at admission.
- **Doctor plus AI model:** one YC company has a nurse and AI walk a patient through symptoms. The AI makes a recommendation and the doctor reviews and approves it. The doctor sees about 4x the patients, and the patient gets a longer, more detailed appointment.
- **Cheap testing:** he likes Sciox (photonics-based blood testing). It started with a mail-in business (a few drops of blood on paper) to prove the business while validating hardware, and the technology could scale down to something like a continuous glucose monitor.
- **Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs):** he recommends everyone try one for a couple of months (Dexcom, or Freestyle Libre). It gives readings roughly every five minutes and changes behavior because the feedback is immediate. Findings: a Fuji apple spikes his blood sugar a lot, and eating a dessert after a big meal affects him less than eating it on an empty stomach.
- **Lifestyle over pills:** much of healthcare is lifestyle change, but the system is incentivized around treating illness ("sick care"), with "no billing code" for lifestyle coaching. He thinks an always-present AI coach could align better with just helping you.

chunks.heading: Regulation, Uber, and routing around slow rules
chunks.text:
On whether regulated industries (energy, healthcare) will improve, Paul says he hopes so, but often people just circumvent regulation. His example: in 2006 he lived in the city, saw how bad cab service was, and effectively had the idea for Uber ("my phone has a GPS, I should be able to press a button and a car shows up"), but dismissed it because of taxi medallions and legality. Uber "just went and did it," and it became legal afterward. He thinks many things will work this way, like people already using ChatGPT as a doctor.

He also sees AI transforming education through fully individualized instruction ("meet every child where they are"), while raising the question of what kids are being educated for.

chunks.heading: Other ideas: construction, robots and better persuasion
chunks.text:
- **Construction as prompting:** housing is a big limiter because construction has become incredibly expensive and almost impossible. He imagines building a house as easy as using an AI art tool, refining the design then pressing Go. He also wants robotic honeybee drone swarms that build fantastical structures impossible with conventional techniques.
- **Humanoid robots:** they look on the way from lab demos, though others are skeptical about training data. He doesn't see data as a fundamental limit; current AI is just inefficient compared to humans, who learn from small amounts of data.
- **Politics and the blind men and the elephant:** he wants AI to help people understand multiple perspectives, since politics makes people think the other side is "stupid and evil." In the parable, each blind man holds a different part of the elephant and either fights or talks and builds a shared picture. He applies this to relationships and marriages too, where failure to communicate is common.
- **Persuasion:** AI is very good at convincing people and will give individualized messaging. He believes in positive-sum outcomes: if you can identify the positive-sum outcome and sell it individually to each person, that's a good use (his example: selling nuclear energy to everyone). He says nuclear fear is not unreasonable (he grew up near a nuclear plant with test sirens), but Chernobyl came from reckless testing and bad design, which greater intelligence can fix.
- **Pessimistic prediction:** he expects things to get a little worse before they get better in political strife and job losses, but thinks a positive vision gets people through.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Gmail's creator explains how startups win. Huge outcomes ride a big technology shift, founder iteration speed beats the starting idea, and incumbents get trapped by their legacy business and caution (Google Video vs YouTube). Much of the talk is AI and free speech politics, which is not business content.

chunks.heading: Gmail was built on a stagnant market, and the lesson was iteration speed
chunks.text:
- Paul says Gmail could innovate so much because web mail had stagnated. Competitors Hotmail and Yahoo Mail were "incredibly clunky": the whole page reloaded on every action, they were covered in ads, and Hotmail's default quota was 2 megabytes.
- He notes an iPhone photo is roughly 5 MB, so those products were far behind. Nobody had improved them in a long time, and if anything they were getting worse.
- His read: big room to innovate exists when incumbents have stopped shipping. He sees no such situation in AI chat interfaces, where Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are all competing hard, so he would not try to compete on interface there.
- Gmail launched April 1, 2004. At the time Google staff were terrified of Microsoft. Twenty years later both are multi-trillion-dollar companies that coexist, and Microsoft's business shifted from the Windows and Office monopoly to enterprise software. His point: big competitive threats rarely play out as expected.

chunks.heading: Google Video lost to YouTube because it was overly cautious
chunks.text:
- Google Video launched before YouTube. Internally the team doubted anyone would upload anything good: "the only thing we could think of is like well probably they're just going to upload like copyrighted content and porn."
- Google Video made uploaders fill out a big form listing actors and directors, as if it were a Hollywood production, then put the video through a review process.
- YouTube simply let people upload and go live, with no gates. It went viral early with copyrighted clips such as the SNL "Lazy Sunday" sketch.
- YouTube later became what Paul calls possibly "the greatest like educational resource that has ever existed". His son uses it for 3D printing and material science.
- Takeaways he draws: unexpected uses are hard to foresee ("in hindsight it's like super easy but ... at the time it's never as easy as it looks"), and process and caution can kill a product against a startup that just ships.

chunks.heading: How Paul stress-tests a startup: the 10-year time machine
chunks.text:
- Startups operate on roughly a 10-year horizon from seed to IPO. DoorDash was funded in 2013 and IPO'd in 2021. Reddit was funded in 2005 and IPOs about 20 years later.
- His exercise: imagine stepping out of a DeLorean in March 2034, clearing the time fog, and asking what changed.
- His core theory: a massive success never happens on its own. It rides an underlying technological shift. Google rode the explosion of the internet. DoorDash and Uber exist because of the smartphone.
- He asks founders which underlying shift lets them become a $100 billion or trillion-dollar company in 10 years.
- Since about 2017 he has found it harder to look 10 years out, and he says he no longer knows what happens in 10 years because AI is approaching an event horizon. In his view 2024 is a pivotal year while things get sorted out.

chunks.heading: What Y Combinator selects for: founders and iteration speed, not ideas
chunks.text:
- Paul says YC does not pick ideas: "we pick the founders and the founders bring the ideas." People wrongly assume YC decides what is hot that year, which he says is never the case.
- Founders often pivot, so the starting idea is frequently not the good one. The aim is people who "are able to move fast and iterate and make intelligent decisions."
- One of the biggest predictors of startup success, in his view, is how quickly a person iterates. A dumb starting idea is fine. Getting stuck on it is not.
- A lot of YC's work is pushing founders to go talk to customers.
- On competition, he says concerns tend to be overblown. His example of a weak pitch: "it's like Gmail but with one extra feature" is not a viable business. A business should not be something a larger competitor can trivially do.
- YC takes a "law of large numbers" approach: a couple hundred startups per batch, so it can make many bets.
- He declines to say what he would build starting out in 2024. The idea has to come from the founder's own experience and insights.

chunks.heading: Why a startup can beat an incumbent: the innovator's dilemma (Perplexity example)
chunks.text:
- Paul likes Perplexity because it iterates quickly, keeps improving the product and keeps engaging users.
- Google's problem is that its search business is hugely profitable, and years of near-monopoly have filled results pages with ads, sometimes a whole first screen of them.
- Perplexity has no legacy business to protect. His rule: if the new business is only 10% as good as the old one, that is terrible for the incumbent but still great for a startup.
- He still concedes that competing directly with Google is hard, and that Perplexity and Google can coexist.
- He is also interested in AI storytelling and media. Within about a year he expects an amateur to produce animation as good as work that currently needs a large budget, such as turning his daughter's fan fiction into animated shows.

chunks.heading: AI changes what being a developer means, and makes prediction harder
chunks.text:
- On whether AI replaces or enhances developers, Paul says "both." The tools make building more accessible, and being a developer will increasingly mean describing what you want to an AI and iterating through dialogue.
- He declines to forecast five years out because "things are moving so quickly."
- His own past forecasting record included mobile, cloud and Facebook. He jokes he picked the wrong TV personality to win the 2016 election, thinking Stephen Colbert rather than Donald Trump.
- On interfaces, he expects the next step beyond chat boxes is an always-available agent: open the camera and microphone and have a real-time conversation about what the camera sees. He thinks Apple is in a strong position because it owns the device in your pocket, though it looked late on models.
- He cautions that a research prototype is very different from a shipped product facing millions of adversarial users, and that deployed products learn from interaction. That is why Google could not just launch something better the day after ChatGPT.

chunks.heading: Email's lasting role and when not to use it
chunks.text:
- Email's strength is that it is universal and owned by no platform: "it's the base layer." When you sign up for Amazon it emails you, it does not DM you on Instagram.
- He is glad other channels (Slack, DMs) take over some communication. His guidance on use:
  - Good for factual things: a document, a receipt.
  - Avoid it for anything complicated.
  - Never use it for a stressful issue.

chunks.heading: AI risk is centralization of power, and open source plus competition is the hedge
chunks.text:
- Paul's main fear is humans using AI for centralized control, not a rogue AI. He gives examples: monitoring everything anyone says, and altering reality in real time, such as faking a video call with a relative.
- He says AI can be either "the most horribly oppressive and dystopian thing we've ever done or ... the best thing we've ever done," and that the outcome is undecided and up to us.
- Because training models needs billions of dollars of compute, AI tends toward centralization. His counter: support many competing AI developers (Google, OpenAI, Facebook, Anthropic) and open-source AI.
- He calls locking AI down in one centralized effort "probably the most dangerous thing we can do." He argues that handing power to experts "acting for the common good" tends to end up like the Soviet Union, because centralized systems reward political skill and the winners are "the most effective Psychopaths." Markets force you to deliver value, which he contrasts with political systems where power can simply be captured.
- He is glad Facebook became "the unexpected hero" for open-source AI and says the thing to watch for is legislation that would prohibit open models. He allows that open-sourcing has legitimate risks and that the debate should stay open.
- He argues an AI's character derives from the society that builds it, so a free society should embed freedom and individual dignity in it.

chunks.heading: Narrative control, free speech, and a "meta narrative"
chunks.text:
- Paul calls freedom of speech the most fundamental freedom, because without it everything else can be lied about. His example is the COVID lab-leak question, which he says he puts at about 95% likely and which people were censored and slandered for raising four years earlier.
- He credits Elon Musk buying Twitter as a major factor in the shift. In his telling, the old Twitter enforced the "institutional narrative" through bans and through the loudest voices being original blue checks aligned with it. Removing that class mattered more than is widely realized.
- He describes how language is used to shut down debate, by labeling a question a racist conspiracy theory so advertisers and platforms justify censorship. He recommends Orwell's *Homage to Catalonia*, in which Orwell's own faction was reclassified as fascist.
- He says most people drawn to these movements have good intentions and respond to incentives, so "it's bad ideas it's bad narratives" rather than bad people. He cites Malthusian zero-sum thinking and the one-child policy as examples.
- His proposed remedy is awareness: a news product that reports from a "meta narrative" view, laying both (or three) narratives side by side on roughly equal footing so people see them as stories. He says he has not pursued this enough.
- He points to Byron Katie's *Loving What Is*, where you identify a painful thought and write turnarounds, and says "you don't let go of the story, the story lets go of you." He calls this awareness "the beginning of alignment," meaning both human and AI alignment.
- On Elon Musk's effectiveness, he points to the Walter Isaacson book: Musk shows up at production bottlenecks and questions assumptions, such as a plastic battery part that turned out not to be needed ("the best part is no part"). Paul thinks that micromanagement gets into the culture.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit recounts joining YC's second batch in 2006 by cold emailing, and making early angel bets like Wufoo for a ~50x return. He explains why he optimizes for learning over safety, why startups are a power-law game, and how YC and Standard Capital pump up founder ambition.

chunks.heading: How Paul got into early Y Combinator
chunks.text:
- Paul read Slashdot, which regularly posted Paul Graham essays. In 2005 PG posted one on the Summer Founders Program, and Paul loved that anyone could apply, with no need to know a founder or have a famous roommate.
- He followed YC from afar at first. His child was in the hospital at the time, so he couldn't take part.
- In fall 2005 PG announced the second batch would run in Mountain View (the first was in Cambridge). Paul cold emailed PG, introduced himself and offered to help.
- PG replied and introduced him to Jessica, who was writing Founders at Work. Paul then started showing up at the batch dinners and meeting the founders.
- The second batch was winter '06, with about 10 companies. In Paul's words, "almost all of them you've never heard of."

chunks.heading: What the early demo days were like
chunks.text:
- Most of venture thought YC was "some kind of a joke with like horrible adverse selection," where no good company would ever apply.
- Demo day was first called Angel Day. The audience was about 20 people, whoever PG and Jessica could convince to show up.
- Presentations were rough. One founder building a database opened a terminal and typed SQL queries.
- One summer '06 team pitched two different ideas because they weren't confident in either.
- Almost no one was writing checks. Paul says the only investors at demo day were himself, PG and Trevor.
- Summer batches were still in Cambridge, so Paul flew to Boston for the summer '06 and summer '07 demo days.
- There was real raw talent (he names Jared's batch), but the ideas were basic. Mostly it was "a website where you can do X," such as rating your professor.

chunks.heading: The Wufoo angel investment and returns
chunks.text:
- One of his first angel investments was Wufoo, an online form builder.
- Paul put in $50K and PG put in $50K, and that was the whole round.
- This was before the SAFE or the capped convertible note existed. It was a literal series seed for a $100K investment.
- They invested at about a $1 million valuation.
- Wufoo was later acquired by SurveyMonkey for "I think about $50 million," which Paul puts at roughly a 50x return.
- He also invested in Anywhere FM and says he was one of the only people on its cap table. He thinks it came from the summer '06 batch.

chunks.heading: Why he invested when almost no one else did
chunks.text:
- Asked why he was smart enough to do it, Paul says he doesn't think he was. His approach: "optimize for learning."
- His logic was that investing some money would teach him something, and it did.
- Playing it overly safe means you never get the experience.
- "Startups are a power law business." It's fine if most investments are bad as long as a couple are very good.

chunks.heading: Why today's YC startups are more ambitious than 2005's
chunks.text:
- Paul's example from a recent demo day: founders planning to manufacture solar cells on the moon. In the early days it was a site for rating professors.
- YC always tried to pump up founders' ambitions. This compounds across batches, because each batch sees what the last one did and raises its own bar.
- YC also attracts more ambitious people, and then pushes them to beat the founders who came before.
- Success brought capital. The original idea was that $20K let people live the grad-student lifestyle for a summer while building a website.
- Now demo day is "a huge feeding frenzy" with rounds of $10-20 million. That funds far bigger ideas, and a rocket company would have been unfundable back then.
- Investors now believe they could be funding the next DoorDash, Stripe or OpenAI, where 25 years ago they were looking at a form-filling tool.
- Paul still sees the same vibe of smart young hackers.
- The one thing he misses is the small size. He could know every company in the batch because they all sat at one dinner table. He can't know a thousand companies.

chunks.heading: Hard tech at YC
chunks.text:
- Paul says he always loved deeper technology.
- His group of hard tech companies included Oklo (small fission reactors, now public), Helion (fusion, which he says is a couple of years from feeding energy onto the grid, and which recently raised another round) and Rigetti (quantum computers, also public now).
- The early YC space also had Trevor's robotics company Anybots, so the dinners happened next to walking robots and a homemade Segway. Paul says this is part of what made early YC cool.
- The first YC batch included Sam (OpenAI), Justin and Emmett (Twitch) and the Reddit founders. Paul's point: "a lot can come out of a small group of people that no one's ever heard of."

chunks.heading: What Paul brings to Standard Capital from early YC
chunks.text:
- Build a community of really ambitious founders and bring them together.
- Push them to be more ambitious: "Why are your goals so sad?" Ask how to turn the company into a $100 billion or trillion dollar company.
- He says this is a lot of the value an investor can add, and it's what founders come for.
- The place is not for people who don't want to build something world changing.
- The goal is to curate the right people so that amazing things can happen, as they did when YC was new and small.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit explains why loss-averse, controlling and slow angel investors are bad for founders, and why good investors write checks fast, diversify and treat the money as gone. He also advises founders to shut down cleanly rather than fake an exit.

chunks.heading: Fundraising: what makes an investor "bad"
chunks.text:
Paul says bad investor behavior mostly comes from aversion to loss. In startups, especially at the early stage, an investor has to accept that most deals will lose money.

- The expected case at seed is that most deals go to zero.
- What Paul looks for is the one deal that returns "a thousand extra turn or hopefully better," which pays for all the zeros.
- That logic is the opposite of real estate or stock investing, where losing everything means something went badly wrong.
- Investors who can't accept this keep trying to defend against loss, and that shows up as bad behavior.

chunks.heading: Skittish diligence and obscure risks
chunks.text:
Paul argues endless diligence is a sign of an unsophisticated investor.

- At an early stage there is always something wrong with the company. If he can't think of five reasons it might fail, he shouldn't invest: "it means I don't have insight," or it's a scam.
- Asking for three meetings, four people on the call, and three-year financial projections from a two-person startup is "silly crap."
- Paul says he has been scammed a couple of times, but it was less than 1% of his money. Losing half a percent to fraud isn't worth ruining the good deals by being paranoid.
- He remembers the era of handing a founder a check after a few minutes' conversation, and says that experience is why founders rated him highly.
- Over-process usually comes from needing to justify a loss to whoever's money you manage ("we did all this diligence, we met them 15 times").
- His "higher order bit" idea: in a number, the leftmost digit matters more than all the others combined. In startups, the one that matters is whether they're building something people want and can grow it into a huge company. Everything else is noise.

chunks.heading: Control, panic and activist investors
chunks.text:
- Trying to control the company also comes from fear of loss. It's worst at the venture stage, when a junior partner's career is tied to one deal and they start "managing the founder." Paul calls that a nightmare for the founder and bad for the company.
- A good investor bets on the team and supports them, and accepts that if the team is no good the money is gone. Being overbearing won't get it back.
- Paul's rule for angels: step one is write the check, step two is "kiss the money goodbye." Mark it at zero. If it comes back, that's great news.
- Never try to recover an investment. A common version is an investor demanding their money back when things go badly, which is "not how it works."
- Founders are already under pressure and don't need an investor emailing weekly about an article they read, or sending random intros ("my neighbor knows about computers").
- He prefers a clean shutdown to a fake positive exit. If a failing startup sells to another failing startup, investors get a tiny slice of equity in an unknown company, more paperwork, and no tax write-off yet because the loss hasn't happened. His advice: pay everyone, shut down, "give me a clean zero."

chunks.heading: Investors with no money, tiny budgets or big egos
chunks.text:
Paul describes several types of bad investor to screen out.

- People with no money who try to be a middleman between a startup and someone who has money.
- People whose budget is tiny, so they meet hundreds of founders to make one investment.
- People who enjoy the power differential of founders coming to pitch them.
- Successful people from another industry who overestimate themselves and think they should tell the "kid asking for money" how things are done.
- Paul's own stance: "What I'm looking for is someone who's going to start a trillion-dollar company, and I've never started a trillion-dollar company. So, I'm looking for someone better than myself." He wants to be convinced the founder knows better than he does, and he's funding them because they're the expert.
- Paul notes YC's internal investor database lets you see how many deals an investor has actually done.

chunks.heading: Why to write many small checks
chunks.text:
Paul explains the diversification logic he gives to people new to angel investing.

- It's very hard to pick the winners early because reality is unpredictable. DoorDash is one of YC's greatest investments, roughly a hundred-billion-dollar company, but at one point it was two weeks from bankruptcy. A slightly different history would have made it a zero.
- Given that uncertainty, the sensible approach is a diversified portfolio rather than one large check.
- Paul points to the Kelly criterion, which as he remembers it suggests about 20 investments.

chunks.heading: Speed, slow processes and adverse selection
chunks.text:
Paul's rule is that speed is always of the utmost importance.

- Slow investors slow you down. A six-month or three-month fundraise is a bad sign, and he doesn't know anyone good who runs that way.
- He says Facebook bought his company in a weekend, and deals don't take months "if you're working with people who are competent and willing to move fast."
- Slow investors suffer adverse selection: no good founder tolerates a slow process, so they only attract the struggling startups with no other choice. That is why their returns are worst.
- Investors who think being slow and careful screens for quality are "shooting themselves in the foot."
- Founders who tolerate a prolonged process are selecting themselves into the bottom of the market. Paul says founders are "actually better off not raising."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit and Dalton discuss how feeds and LLMs can fill a founder's head with "sand". Paul tells the origin of the like button at FriendFeed and argues for time limits, regular disconnects, in-person peers, and selling to real customers as a reality check.

chunks.heading: Technology creates new "info hazards," and the founder's defense is staying grounded
chunks.text:
Paul describes info hazards as the way each new medium (television, cable, forums, feeds, LLMs) can warp what people believe or how they feel. His core claim: "everyone is going a little bit crazy, probably," and the more time spent staring at screens, especially feeds, the worse it gets.

- **TV:** two or three channels meant everyone got "brainwashed the same." Cable created filter bubbles, so people started sharing culture with strangers far away more than with neighbors.
- **Online communities:** you can find like-minded people, but you can also fool yourself into thinking fringe opinions are popular.
- **Self-reinforcing bubbles:** "everyone agrees with everyone else, and anyone who disagrees gets kicked out of the community."
- **New media, no immune system:** each new form of media spreads like a virus. Young people who grew up with it develop better natural immunity (for example, spotting AI slop that older users share). Society also develops norms and guardrails over time, as with the gin carts of early distilled alcohol.

chunks.heading: Why feeds are uniquely dangerous (Paul's FriendFeed insider view)
chunks.text:
Paul helped build "the sausage factory." He lays out the mechanics:

- A feed is a non-stop drip of bite-sized, interesting content, so you are always incentivized to take "one more hit."
- There is no end. With a newspaper you finish and move on; with a feed "you yourself have to close the window."
- The machine reads what engages you (even just pausing on content) and feeds you more of it. This reinforces whatever you already feel.
- The most engaging content tends to be alarming, so doom scrolling is demoralizing and can leave you depressed.
- His jar analogy: rocks, then small rocks, then sand. Feeds are sand. If you fill your head with sand first, "there's no room for anything of substance."
- His remedy for a bad feed state: close the window, exercise, go for a run and disconnect.

chunks.heading: Origin of the like button at FriendFeed
chunks.text:
Paul's account of how the first like button came about:

- In 2007 he co-founded FriendFeed with Bret Taylor and others. It aggregated feeds (RSS, YouTube, other social products) and added comments.
- As a small, young network it lacked users. Posting with no feedback is demoralizing, "like you're talking to an empty room."
- The like was designed as a one-click comment: minimum effort, but "if you put something out in the world and you get like 10 likes, that's great," and it encourages you to keep posting.
- FriendFeed created the first like button. Facebook added theirs about a year later. Paul says Facebook internally had a similar feature called the "awesome button" that never launched, probably because it sounded embarrassing.
- Emoji reactions are a generalization of the like.

chunks.heading: LLM filter bubbles and AI validation
chunks.text:
Paul argues LLMs create a new kind of info hazard:

- Models are very affirming ("You're absolutely right") and don't push back as much as they should, so you can go down a road with no one telling you "that's kind of crazy. Maybe take a break."
- He says they seem trained to earn a thumbs up from the user, and there are many shades between power user and "AI psychosis."
- LLMs have created "a new class of crackpots" who believe they have solved physics or found a theory of everything.
- No immune system exists yet and norms for healthy use are undefined. Paul says "the jury is out" on whether asking an LLM about every micro decision is appropriate.
- His advice: be especially wary of an LLM validating big life decisions or fantastical claims about your abilities. Never hold the technology up as a mirror of yourself: "don't do that" (asking it who you are or whether it understands you).
- The same applies to social media: your audience eventually "captures you," and your brain gets "RL'd to produce social media content" that may not be good for you.

chunks.heading: Practical rules for using feeds and LLMs healthily
chunks.text:
Paul's tactics for founders:

- **Set limits:** "a little bit seems to be okay, but all day long is definitely bad." For feeds he gets the most value in the first 10 minutes, with diminishing returns and accumulating damage after.
- **Come up for air:** take gaps, such as staying away over the weekend. A good test is "can you disconnect?" He says you can function without talking to Claude every 20 minutes.
- **Go outdoors without earbuds:** you don't have to listen to podcasts all the time. A walk or run is good for you whatever else you do.
- **Use the tools for learning:** he is convinced YouTube made him smarter. He says TikTok did too (exercise, personal health, running and swimming tips, music theory), and he is "a better person" for it. The problem is only when usage cripples you, for example if he spent all day on TikTok and couldn't hold down a job.
- **Remember it isn't real life:** feeds are not your life and almost nothing happening on X matters. Paul tells his kids that Instagram feels real and "kind of isn't."
- **Expect downsides:** no important new technology is entirely good, so aim for a healthy ground state on a regular basis.

chunks.heading: Staying grounded as a founder: in-person peers and real customers
chunks.text:
Paul's view that "the word that comes to mind is grounded":

- **In-person time:** Standard Capital's group office hours format forces founders to meet in person rather than stare at screens. Being alone behind a screen makes it easy "to go a little bit crazy," while face-to-face interaction "brings more sanity."
- **Real peers:** a Slack channel of real founders you know is far more helpful than only having X followers. If your startup peers are anonymous accounts with anime profile pictures, "you could get in a pretty weird spot."
- **Customers as grounding:** a founder can convince themselves "everyone wants my product," but trying to sell it reveals the truth. "Actually trying to sell products is a form of grounding. Because when you ask people for money, they say no."
- **Versus LLM validation:** Claude will say your idea for "french fry salad" is awesome, but only trying to sell it tells you for real.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit and Dalton Caldwell of Standard Capital look back at how YC funded hard tech (Ginkgo, Helion, Rigetti, OpenAI) when investors ridiculed it. Paul stresses founder quality, a clear path to a product, and proving yourself in stages, treating each fundraise as a new "miracle."

chunks.heading: YC's early hard tech bets worked, against wide ridicule
chunks.text:
- Paul remembers it as "a little bit crazy" at the time, because YC was long known only for things you could build with a website.
- Sam recruited hard tech companies including Ginkgo Bioworks, Oklo, Rigetti and Helion. Paul was a YC partner to Oklo, Rigetti and Helion, which were all in one batch.
- His main lesson in hindsight: "it worked". Several of those companies are now public.
- It showed YC could fund more than websites. It also showed the startup world that you can build just about anything, and that new technology can come to market.
- Example: Helion is building nuclear fusion, long science fiction. Paul says it is a couple of years from delivering power to customers.

chunks.heading: Why hard tech worked: great founders, YC supplies company-building
chunks.text:
- Paul's belief is that a lot comes down to the right people, with real ambition, who are real builders.
- YC never brings the technical expertise. "If we have to tell you how to build the fusion reactor, it's not going to happen."
- What YC does help with is everything else: building a company and raising capital. Paul says that goes well beyond the details of the technology.
- Billion to One is the example. It is his pick for YC's most successful bio company, and it IPO'd at the end of last year. Its investor updates laid out the plan years ahead. The one from around 2020 said it would IPO in 2025, and it hit that.

chunks.heading: Harder startups can improve your odds
chunks.text:
- Paul says "counterintuitively", harder startups can give you a better chance. They are more inspiring and exciting, and they face less competition.
- A low-ambition idea attracts many other low-ambition people competing on the same thing. Outrageous ideas are avoided by most people.
- SpaceX is the extreme example. 20 years ago, trying it was "pure insanity".

chunks.heading: OpenAI as a hard tech bet
chunks.text:
- Paul points to OpenAI, started at YC, as another example of hard tech ambition that looked crazy at the time.
- The idea that a startup would develop AGI was "pretty laughable".
- It was up against Google, which had all the data, money, researchers and computers. OpenAI was a small nonprofit research lab without a product.

chunks.heading: How this shapes what Standard Capital funds
chunks.text:
- Paul applies the same rules as at YC: great founders with a lot of ambition and a path from here to there.
- He wants a clear route: deliver a product today, scale, raise much more money, and prove yourself as you go.
- He does not want "we're going to do this thing and we don't know how".
- A second benefit is community. Bringing credible hard tech founders together lets them compare notes. Few peers have built a late-stage hard tech company.
- His framing: you are the average of the five people around you, so Standard wants to surround founders with impressive peers who raise each other up.

chunks.heading: Hard tech is a chain of miracles, financed in stages
chunks.text:
- Paul calls the "series of miracles" frame a great one. A hard tech company succeeds by proving it is a miracle worker.
- Tesla is his example: the Roadster, Model S, Model 3 and self-driving were each a miracle. The company chains impossible things on top of each other, and each one increases its ability to raise capital. SpaceX works the same way, with Starship as the new miracle.
- Investors are more excited to back a proven miracle worker than a fresh one.
- The practical lesson for founders: don't expect investors to see the brilliance of your idea and fund the whole end state at once. Keep succeeding, and at each stage raise enough money to reach the next level.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit explains how wealth is actually created (positive-sum exchange, marketplaces, good decisions) and turns it into a startup filter. Ask where the wealth is created, aim for unbounded markets, and create far more value than you capture.

chunks.heading: Wealth creation as the first test for a startup idea
chunks.text:
- Paul says a key question when he evaluates a startup is "where is the wealth created?"
- He argues most people, and most politicians, have no real concept of how wealth is created.
- His example of a category with no visible wealth creation is NFTs, and some crypto token businesses. He describes the model as "we create this token and then we sell it to someone else" who sells it to someone else, with no point where value is created.
- He advises founders to understand how their startup creates wealth. The more wealth created for users and customers, the better. Not having a good answer to this is "a problem."

chunks.heading: Marketplaces create wealth by connecting supply and demand
chunks.text:
- Paul says marketplaces are underappreciated. Many of the most valuable companies are marketplaces under the hood. Google and Facebook are both advertising marketplaces that bring buyers and sellers together on a platform.
- His mechanism: a producer makes a widget for $10, and a consumer would happily pay $100. Even with a million consumers, if buyer and seller can't find each other, the transaction never happens.
- A marketplace creates wealth by connecting producer and consumer. It is a positive-sum exchange where both parties end up better off. The marketplace typically collects a percentage of the revenue.
- Examples he endorses:
  - eBay: people have junk packed away in garages and storage, and someone else wants it.
  - Airbnb: Joe and Brian had a spare bedroom and rented it out during a design conference to make rent. It turned dead space into cash for the host and cheap lodging for the traveler.
  - Whatnot: a "modern eBay competitor" and one of his best investments at YC. He says many people make a living selling on its live streams.

chunks.heading: Positive-sum vs zero-sum thinking
chunks.text:
- Paul says many people hold a zero-sum view of wealth: a fixed amount exists, so someone with a billion dollars must have stolen it. He says this is especially common at the socialist end of the spectrum.
- The positive-sum view sees a founder who created billions in wealth and kept a slice. Typically a founder who reaches IPO owns about 10% of the company they created.
- He compares the zero-sum view to a Scrooge McDuck money bin: "if only we could bust open Scrooge McDuck's money bin, then everyone could be wealthy." He says that approach has been tried and "generally ends in mass starvation."
- He cites Paul Graham's example of buying an old car, fixing it up and selling it for more. Labor produces more value than it cost, and no one was cheated.
- Wealth comes from physical labor and also from good decisions. His own business is the example: good investments are "fabulously profitable," and only wrong ones go to zero. The decision is where the wealth creation happens.

chunks.heading: Pick markets with no ceiling
chunks.text:
- After "where's the wealth creation?", his next question is whether it has a limit. This ties to finite versus infinite markets.
- A weak idea takes all the revenue from an old business worth about $3 billion. He says you're "probably not doing a whole lot of wealth creation there."
- A strong idea sits in a massive, growing opportunity. When Google started in the '90s the internet was still small, so the value of organizing it was limited by its size. As the internet grew 10x, 100x and 1,000x, Google's opportunity to connect people to information and services grew with it. He says Google has "infinite potential for wealth creation."
- He says AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have no real limit on wealth creation because they create intelligence. He calls intelligence a fundamental ingredient of wealth: it leads to new products, curing diseases, fixing environmental issues and going into space.

chunks.heading: Value creation vs value capture
chunks.text:
- Paul frames success as doing both value creation and value capture.
- He says founders often focus only on how to capture value. If you aren't creating value, capturing it is hard, and if you manage it you're "a parasite." He says "we don't want to fund parasites" and wants companies creating massive value.
- The more value you create, the easier it is to capture some fraction and grow a huge business.
- Value creation without capture is also possible. His example is Linux: Linus created enormous value but gave it away, so he captured only a tiny fraction, mostly through fame.
- His ideal: "the optimal startup is one that is creating infinite value and then capturing, you know, 10% of it."
- A way to check: compare the value customers get with the value the startup keeps. Google drives customers to sites and helps businesses get found, and the value captured by the company is a tiny fraction of the benefit to users.

chunks.heading: Be 10x better, and ask whether cheaper grows demand
chunks.text:
- Paul says creating value doesn't mean being the lowest-cost option. Being slightly cheaper than a competitor "is not creating value."
- He wants a product that is "not just like 10% better, but like 10x better." The best combination is a product that is both better and cheaper.
- A follow-up test: when it gets cheaper, does that grow demand?
  - SpaceX: as launch cost falls, new possibilities open, such as asteroid mining companies and hotels on the moon, which only work if launch costs drop.
  - AI: GPUs, built for video games, made matrix multiplication cheap. He says the video game industry accidentally set the foundation for modern AI by driving that cost down.
- His closing advice: create more value than you capture, and have a clear idea of where your startup creates wealth.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit explains why the information-gathering and coordination work of middle managers is what LLMs do well, drawing on Google's early flat-org experiments. He argues startups should go AI-native, using AI as a cognitive multiplier to monitor work, and focus on the people who create value.

chunks.heading: AI as a replacement for middle management
chunks.text:
Paul argues that the core of middle management, "gathering information from people and then combining it and then passing along to the person above," is work AI can do. He frames the trend as "AI eats management."
- People doing the actual work, especially physical work, are still required. The people coordinating that work are the ones who can be replaced.
- He calls this counterintuitive. Conventional wisdom says the least experienced people get replaced first.
- Gathering and organizing information is "exactly the kind of things that LLMs are great at."
- Monitoring and measuring is a big part of management, and AI is very good at it.
- Some founders in Paul's portfolio (funded but not yet announced) are already saying they don't need managers.
- He cites Coinbase as a public company that has officially said it has no more pure managers.

chunks.heading: What a manager actually does, from first principles
chunks.text:
Paul describes management as a coordination role: "When you have a bunch of people working together, you need to make sure they're kind of pointed in the same direction." It also includes making sure everyone is showing up and doing their job.
- An early Google belief was that with really great engineers you need less management. Paul says he thinks that is still true.
- He points to Nvidia, where Jensen Huang has something like 100 direct reports. Paul doesn't remember the exact number, but says it shows a wide span of control is possible.
- Paul agrees the pieces of the job can be unbundled: checking what everyone does, and the emotional-support side. AI can plausibly cover both.
- On emotional support, he notes friends who switched from human therapists to AI. A human therapist "will inevitably insert their own issues," while AI is "infinitely good at listening" and supportive. He sees no reason the same dynamic can't play out in the workplace.
- What AI doesn't replace: Paul concedes you still need someone monitoring performance and handling the inevitable HR issues that come with humans. That was the lesson from Google's first no-managers experiment, though he adds that the setup "worked fine for me."

chunks.heading: Google's no-managers experiment
chunks.text:
Paul was at Google in the early days (around 2001) when Larry Page tried removing engineering managers.
- Larry was frustrated that Google was moving too slowly.
- His solution was to get rid of all engineering managers. Engineers became tech leads on projects, and everyone reported up to the VP of engineering.
- It lasted until about 200 engineers, with roughly 200 people reporting to one VP of engineering.
- That was the point where it broke, and Google brought engineering directors back.
- Paul says Google went through "a few different cycles" of this, so the pattern repeated.
- His read on why it broke: some people needed more hands-on management, and someone has to monitor performance and deal with HR issues.

chunks.heading: How to replace managers with AI in practice
chunks.text:
Paul's approach is the "AI native" one: as a startup, "you just keep scaling and fixing the problems as they occur with AI," solving each problem with AI.
- His mental model is to treat AI as a cognitive multiplier. Ask how you would do the job if you had unlimited time, then give the AI those same instructions, because it effectively has unlimited time.
- Concrete tactic he agrees with: use Claude to run a loop that reads literally everything each person in the organization is doing (check-ins, code) and summarizes it into a chunk you can make sense of, in real time, every day.
- One example he relays: an executive at a large tech company vibe-coded agents to do the work of middle managers. That gave a real-time window into what every individual contributor was doing, with immediate feedback, and the team moved much faster.
- Paul found it notable that this came from someone building it on the ground.

chunks.heading: Implications for how large companies can grow
chunks.text:
Paul speculates that removing management layers changes how big a company can get while staying fast.
- Historically, big companies get "complex and inefficient and political" because of layers of middle management that add "confusion and slowness."
- If AI replaces those layers, in theory organizations could grow much larger without the usual decay.
- Anthropic is his possible example, flagged as speculation: it keeps launching major products "that seem to murder a batch of startups every week or so."
- His theory is that Anthropic uses its AI tools internally so that relatively small teams can ship high-impact products.
- His overall prediction: focus attention and resources on whoever creates the value. Everything will move faster "because we won't have all the layers of confusion that are introduced by middle management."

chunks.heading: Would AI managers make people happier?
chunks.text:
Paul is optimistic that AI managers would make work better for the people being managed.
- Often "you hear stories of people who hate their manager." Humans bring their own issues to work.
- An AI manager could be "always available, who always listens, who's always fair, who isn't injecting their own politics or anything into the decision."
- He argues this could make people happier in their future jobs, and says it is "guaranteed."
- A shared observation he agrees with: no one says they love being 10 layers away from the CEO.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit explains which startups AI labs will run over and which stay defensible. Building on a lab's roadmap, or on workarounds for today's model limits, is a trap. Network effects and existing distribution are the moat when software becomes trivially clonable.

chunks.heading: Startups most at risk are those building on a lab's roadmap
chunks.text:
- Paul says startups building directly on someone else's roadmap, such as Anthropic's, "are going to get run over."
- He cites Google as precedent: it "did kill a lot of startups," especially those adjacent to something it already did. The Gmail example: "it's like Gmail, but it has one extra feature. That's out of business."
- He wants a product that isn't immediately adjacent to a lab's or incumbent's business, with some kind of wall that would be very difficult for them to overcome.
- Labs are heading toward public markets, possibly with trillion-dollar market caps, and will be "super hungry for revenue." A business making $100 million that is easy for someone else to take is exposed.

chunks.heading: The "turkey graph" startup
chunks.text:
- Paul uses the "graph of the turkey's well-being": a thousand and one days of a Thanksgiving turkey's life that look wonderful until the day its head gets chopped off.
- A turkey graph startup has customers and revenue today but isn't defensible, and a lab or competitor can end it suddenly.
- He says building something people want is not enough if the business can be taken from you.
- He says it is annoying when investors ask "what if Google does this?", but argues the question now has teeth because the models keep improving.

chunks.heading: Betting against model progress
chunks.text:
- Paul says some startups are implicitly betting that the models won't get smarter.
- Building workflows, adapters, guardrails and middleware around today's model limitations is a short bet on the labs. Next year's model may not need any of it, or may produce it on its own.
- The analogy is "googledogs.com powered by Google," a startup that only works if Google stays bad at searching for dogs.
- The question to ask: is next year's model going to make you more successful, or eliminate the need for your business?

chunks.heading: Software is about to become clonable
chunks.text:
- Historically software was expensive, slow and painful to build. A complex product was hard to catch up with because the incumbent had the customers, engineers and user base.
- Paul predicts that with the new coding models, "probably next year just about any piece of software will be clonable." If your whole product is software, you're in trouble even if the labs never clone you.
- Cloning could come from an agent: someone's open-claw agent doesn't want to pay for your software, so it clones it, makes an open-source version and shares it with other people's agents. He expects this next year.
- A pure software business whose moat is that it's hard to build or clone "is going to have a bad time."

chunks.heading: Diagnostic: compete with yourself using next year's model
chunks.text:
- Imagine you can press a button and say "clone Microsoft Office," or clone whatever your product is.
- Picture yourself as an ambitious, smart 19-year-old joining Y Combinator next year who wants to take down someone else's business with that future AI. What would you do?
- Assume you already have the future AI, then compete against yourself.

chunks.heading: What is defensible: network effects and existing usage
chunks.text:
- Paul says the best businesses have always had network effects. The test: if you could open-source your product and give it away without much difference, it's defensible.
- DoorDash example: even a perfect clone of the app is worthless without the restaurants, drivers and customers.
- He says you want "a product where the strength comes from the fact that everyone is already using it." Those are incredibly hard to displace.
- Ticketmaster example: people have long wanted to replace it, but distribution agreements and similar ties make it very difficult to displace.
- Regulation can also protect a business, and startups can get a head start by owning data, users and customers where it's harder for labs to go (regulatory, technical or other barriers).
- Regulatory protection may erode too. Uber was technically illegal when it started, did it anyway and got the law changed afterward, and Paul thinks AGI presents opportunities to circumvent some regulations.

chunks.heading: What an established company should do
chunks.text:
- Paul's first answer for a Series B SaaS company: "I'd panic," then it depends on the business.
- He frames AI as a wave: you are either pushed forward by it or smashed by it.
- The task is to work out how the models help improve and grow your business faster, using the tools aggressively and staying ahead of any competitor.
- Internet-era lesson: media distribution businesses (CDs, Blockbuster, newspapers, bookstores) were crushed and had little move other than pivoting. Businesses whose distribution the internet didn't touch, like car companies, were largely unaffected. Banks survived partly because of regulation.
- Incumbents often haven't needed to innovate in so long that they don't know how. He says Sears had the pieces to be Amazon (cities, delivery infrastructure, a catalog business) but lacked the capacity to evolve.

chunks.heading: Why AI grows the pie
chunks.text:
- Paul says wealth comes down to energy and intelligence, and AI is on the cusp of "10xing the amount of intelligence."
- He expects more medical progress in the next 10 to 20 years than at any other time in our lifetimes, along with new materials and a changed understanding of science and reality.
- He thinks energy will also open up, driven by the need to scale it and by new technologies. He says we're going to 10x total wealth, creating more opportunity than has ever existed.
- He says "every problem is a physics problem if you boil it down enough," a mix of physics and engineering. With unlimited engineers and unlimited energy, nearly every problem is solvable.
- Recycling example: it's a scam today because turning plastic into something new is hard, but with abundant energy you could incinerate trash and reuse the atoms, so out comes new raw material.
- He admits he doesn't know for certain that startups will survive and allows that AGI could "turn us all into paperclips," but says Standard Capital is betting that it won't.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A Standard Capital chat on startup hiring. Paul Buchheit (Google employee 23, Gmail creator, FriendFeed founder) explains how he interviewed at early Google, using a hard open problem that surfaced Noam Shazeer, and why you should hire people who make you better.

chunks.heading: Hire only after product-market fit, when work exceeds capacity
chunks.text:
- Paul says to start hiring once you have product-market fit and are ready to grow the company, and not before.
- Hiring before product-market fit makes it harder to find product-market fit: "the larger the team is, the slower you can change."
- Employees get nervous when the founders change direction. They have to be managed and have their feelings handled, and they have to be told why the company pivoted from thing A to thing B.
- Once there is product-market fit, he wants hiring to accelerate growth.
- His trigger for flipping to hiring is having "more work than you can possibly handle" because the company is growing so fast.
- Paul and the other speaker describe YC's internal startup guide, which listed "don't hire" as one of its first rules. Founders who had just raised money often said "Great, we raised money. It's time to start hiring."
- Paul says there was "true wisdom" in the rule. Hiring someone good slows you down immensely, and a hire onto a startup that hasn't figured it out leaves you with a person to manage and reassure.

chunks.heading: Why hiring too early creates morale problems
chunks.text:
- A new employee joining a pre-product-market-fit startup has made a big bet on it. Good employees have many other options.
- If you recruit them, you have to sell them on the vision and on the reality of the company growing fast and becoming big.
- Paul recalls many office hours where founders said their employees wanted to quit or thought the founders were doing a bad job, and asked what to tell them.
- His answer was to ask whether the founders were doing a good job: "the best story is the true story."
- When the company wasn't taking off, those founders had constant employee morale issues.

chunks.heading: Do the job yourself before hiring for it
chunks.text:
- Paul says founders often hire for something they cannot do themselves.
- Founders in that position don't know how to interview for the role or how to manage the person.
- A common result is that they hire someone from a big company with an impressive resume, who then spends 6 to 12 months failing. The founder is frustrated and can't tell whether the person is wrong or the job is simply hard.
- His advice: the founder should first do the job themselves, then find someone who can do it better.

chunks.heading: Hiring at early Google
chunks.text:
- Paul was employee 23 at Google and found the job on Slashdot, a site he describes as "news for nerds, stuff that matters" for Linux enthusiasts.
- He was a Linux enthusiast looking for a company building on Linux, which was rare in the 90s. He found about six such companies, applied to all of them, and got one job offer.
- He says he didn't appreciate at the time how special Google was. He credits the company's success partly to hiring super talented people.
- Google's interviews were technical: coding on a whiteboard, algorithm questions and similar.
- Paul's own habit was to ask candidates about one of the hardest problems he was working on, one he didn't know the answer to.

chunks.heading: Interviewing with a problem you haven't solved: the "did you mean" story
chunks.text:
- In 2000 Paul built Google's "did you mean" spell corrector. He is not good at spelling, and the logs showed he wasn't alone: he estimates probably half of queries were misspelled. Fixing spelling was one of the easiest ways to improve quality.
- His first version used a spell correction library and "was not brilliant." He believed a statistical model could work out what the user meant.
- After several weeks his own version was "okay but not brilliant." He started using the problem as an interview question, hoping to find someone better.
- Most answers from the many engineers he asked ranged from mediocre to terrible.
- One candidate, Noam Shazeer, was already ahead of Paul's thinking during the interview. Paul told the team they had to hire him.
- In his first two weeks Noam built the "did you mean" corrector that Google still uses, which Paul calls "basically the greatest spell corrector that has ever existed."
- About 17 years later Noam was a key author of "Attention Is All You Need" (the transformer paper). Paul notes his interview question was, in hindsight, to build a small language model.
- Paul says to pose the hardest questions you don't know the answer to, and to look for people who are smarter than you.

chunks.heading: Hire people better than you
chunks.text:
- Paul cites the saying: "A's hire A's and B's hire C's."
- His reasoning: people who aren't that good often know it, and find smarter people threatening, so they hire people who are less good.
- Someone who is smart and ambitious wants to be surrounded by people who inspire them and from whom they can learn.
- In any interview he asks himself whether it is a person he can learn a lot from.
- His basic end-of-interview test: ask "what did I learn?" If the answer is nothing, it was a bad interview.

chunks.heading: Interviewing Ilya Sutskever for OpenAI
chunks.text:
- Paul says OpenAI was created at Y Combinator in 2015 and was originally called YC Research. The reasoning was that AI was happening but was locked up inside Google, and YC wanted it open to the world and to YC startups, who would otherwise be in trouble.
- Sam emailed Paul and the other speaker to say Ilya was a great candidate for OpenAI co-founder. He asked them to interview Ilya and give a thumbs up before moving forward.
- Paul had been into neural nets in the 90s and says they always seemed like obviously the right way to do AI, though he wasn't smart enough to make them work.
- He asked Ilya why neural nets started working, given that in the 90s they were a dead end. Things changed in 2012 with AlexNet.
- Ilya's explanation included something basic that Paul found surprising. As Paul recalls it (and says he doesn't know if it's true), the field had been initializing weights with random numbers between roughly 0 and 0.2, and the right choice was a random number between -1 and 1.
- Paul's takeaway about research: often someone does something arbitrary and everyone else copies it without questioning it.
- In 2015 Ilya said that AI was the most important problem in the world, that we would have superhuman-level intelligence to solve all sorts of problems, and that it would change how we live. This was before AI belief was common.
- Paul says most founders say bold things in YC interviews and none of it happens (he mentions Web3), but every so often a founder describes the reality we now live in. Ilya's claims were "dead on" with hindsight.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buchheit's 2014 Startup School Europe talk argues that the real technology is the patterns in your head, and shares six defaults for founders: stay open, silence inner voices, accept setbacks, pick the interesting path, love what you do, and ignore the impossible. Mostly mindset, with concrete examples from Gmail, Google, Justin.tv/Twitch and Uber.

chunks.heading: Seeking deep appeal and the danger of experience
chunks.text:
- Paul advises startups to seek deep appeal: "create something that a few people love, even if most people don't get it right away." He notes the business is "defined by outliers."
- His first pattern is "I don't know anything." If he believes he already has the answer, he isn't open to learning larger truths. Founders should own their own programming rather than take his word as authority.
- Experience is a danger because it tells you an idea won't work. Naive, young founders often start the most successful companies because "they just don't know any better," and they're often too arrogant to listen to those who do. What didn't work before may work now, and what worked before may not work again.
- The best opportunities "live in our collective blind spots." They look like bad ideas or unimportant ones. If everyone could see the opportunity, someone else would already have taken it.
- Example: in 1997 Larry and Sergey tried to sell Google for a million dollars and found no buyer. The conventional wisdom was that search was neither important nor valuable.
- Dogma and ideology are worse than experience. They give you answers and put boundaries around your thinking. He suspects this is why more ideological societies are less innovative: you can't find missed opportunities if you can't wander outside conventional thinking.
- From the inside, dogma "looks like truth and reality." That includes logic and reason: "If you believe yourself to be a rational person, then you're in the trap."

chunks.heading: Kill the daemon processes: clearing the voices of doubt
chunks.text:
- Paul's second pattern is "Kill all daemon processes." He uses the operating-system analogy: background programs that run out of control and eat memory and CPU, which is why a reboot often makes a machine work better.
- The brain equivalent is looping voices of doubt, anger and self-loathing. They may be internalized voices of parents, peers, the media or random people online, or they may pose as your own voice. They show up whenever you take a risk or move in a new direction.
- Building a new product often means years on something most people doubt. That is hard "with a head full of noise."
- Example: before Gmail launched, many people inside Google thought the project should be scrapped. One notable executive predicted it would never reach a million users.
- The practice:
  - Stop, observe your breath, and enjoy a moment of stillness.
  - The voices that keep interrupting the silence are the runaway processes. Keep dismissing them until none are left.
  - Use spare moments for this instead of "Flappy Bird or Facebook." It's the practice that matters, even when it doesn't always succeed. Walking in nature also helps.
- The voices resist because asserting their own importance is how they survive, and they keep coming back.

chunks.heading: "Yes, and thank you": turning setbacks into advantage
chunks.text:
- The third pattern is a default response to events: "Yes, and thank you."
- Life rarely goes the way you want. Taking risks means plans often won't work out, and keeping life narrow and risk-free doesn't prevent that either. You can get angry and stuck, or accept and move forward, "assuming that whatever happened is somehow for the best."
- He calls this a great predictor of startup success. All startups face setbacks; some use them to their advantage, and others "keep slamming their head against the same wall."
- Example: Uber turned the London taxi strike into a huge growth opportunity.
- In his own life, many of the best things are rooted in some of the worst events, and he wouldn't have one without the other.
- It's about small decisions more than big ones. He treats every daily setback or disappointment as a gift, however improbable that seems at the time. He says the pattern has an "almost magical way of transforming reality and maintaining the forward flow of life."

chunks.heading: Choosing the more interesting path: how he picks startups
chunks.text:
- The fourth pattern: choose the more interesting path. He says it is a big part of how he decides which startups to invest in.
- Justin.tv example (early 2007):
  - His first response was to laugh and ask if they were serious. The plan was for Justin Kan to attach a camera to his head and stream it live, 24/7.
  - He invested anyway because he was curious what would happen, and the founders seemed to genuinely believe they were on to something.
  - First came trolling. Then anyone could stream their life. Most of it was boring or possibly illegal, but video game streaming caught on, and the company became Twitch.tv to focus on competitive gaming.
  - Twitch's average daily viewer watches over 100 minutes per day, and it is the 4th largest source of US Internet traffic after Netflix, Google and Apple. He says he had no idea that would happen.
- Interestingness signals unexplored or under-explored territory. A known outcome isn't interesting, and pure randomness like gambling isn't either. Great startups sit in "a space of productive uncertainty."
- Same logic when he joined Google in 1999: he expected the much larger Alta Vista to squash it, but the people were very smart and he expected to learn a lot.
- Redefine success to include learning something interesting and "I can guarantee success." A startup with only one definition of success is "setting yourself up for failure."
- He calls it tragic how many people sacrifice their lives to a startup they don't care about, chasing external success they'll likely never reach.

chunks.heading: Love what you do, not "do what you love"
chunks.text:
- The fifth pattern: "Love what you do." He calls "do what you love" mostly bad advice because it pushes people to grind through life chasing unattainable goals like being a movie star or a billionaire founder. Even those who make it often find the reality nothing like they imagined.
- "Do what you love is in the future. Love what you do is right now." It guides small moment-to-moment decisions and is less about changing what you do than how you do it.
- A goal-oriented, extrinsic mindset treats the time before completion as an annoying obstacle. On something difficult, uncertain and long, like building a company, that gambles away a big chunk of your life. It can also push you to pick smaller, more realistic goals, and it's unpleasant.
- His Google hours came from genuinely loving building things, not from pressure: "They weren't whipping us." He typically enjoyed at least 80% of his day.
- What you love isn't fixed. Example: he used to hate running. After reading a book arguing we are born to run, he tried running just for fun, focused on the quality of each step and dropped the goal-completion aspect. He learned to enjoy it quickly and now orients his whole relationship with fitness toward enjoyment.
- An intrinsic approach improves the quality of effort, which tends to bring greater extrinsic rewards too. Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation are best when pointed the same direction.
- Startups involve grinding work: "It's like having a baby. It's 5% cute, adorable moments, and 95% dirty diapers and vomit." The key to loving the unpleasant moments is meaning. If you believe in the mission, hard times take on a more heroic quality.
- Daily plans must be immediate and actionable (write code, talk to users), but he thinks a meaningful, inspiring vision matters too.

chunks.heading: A healthy disregard for the impossible
chunks.text:
- The sixth pattern, borrowed from Google: "Maintain a healthy disregard for the impossible." He thinks Larry Page learned it as a kid at summer camp, and he sees it as the company's innovative spirit.
- Early Google was a tiny, unknown startup. He had to explain it as "Yahoo minus all of the features other than search," and people gave him a look that said "I'm sorry you can't get a real job." Inside, absurdly ambitious ideas made it feel like they'd take over the world.
- Examples from Larry:
  - Store and search the whole web in memory when the machines had only 1/4 GB of RAM. It was unrealistic then, but Moore's law moved fast and they did it, "but only because everyone's thinking was already oriented in that direction."
  - Self-driving cars that deliver hamburgers. That hasn't happened yet, but he bets it will.
- He finds potentially impossible goals more inspiring than realistic ones: "I'd rather fail at something awesome, than succeed at something inconsequential."
- Gmail example: when he decided to write the Gmail interface in Javascript, nearly everyone who knew Javascript or browsers said it was a bad idea, since it had been tried and ended in disaster. He was in an environment where doing impossible things was encouraged. After launch, "the impossible quickly became the new normal," changing how people think about web apps.

chunks.heading: Startups as machines for self-interest, and the "full-stack hacker" mission
chunks.text:
- He sees startups as more than a clever way to make money: "machines for harnessing the fire of human self-interest, creating a self-sustaining reaction capable of rapidly transforming the world." Self-interest is often treated as dirty, but "NASA didn't get to the moon by vilifying gravity."
- Saying business is all about money is "like saying that rockets are all about rocket fuel." You need fuel to leave the launch pad, but that misses the machine's purpose. Among the truly significant founders he has known, "there's always a larger purpose."
- His impossible goal: for the first time we have the technology and resources to provide adequate food, housing, education and healthcare for everyone using only a fraction of labor and resources, which would end "wage-slavery." He says he chooses to work rather than has to, and believes everyone deserves that freedom. He argues it is also economically superior, so everyone would have more wealth.
- Many people are as brilliant as Steve Jobs, but likely lacked great parents, amazing teachers, an environment where innovation was the norm, or a Steve Wozniak down the street. "Economically, we don't need more jobs. We need more Steve Jobs." Setting everyone free enables outliers everywhere. The impossible part: "First we have to learn how to get along with each other, and with ourselves."
- He is looking for "full-stack hackers" who understand that the same patterns exist everywhere. "Capitalism is a technology," like the internal combustion engine, valuable but improvable, and so are government and religion.
- Founders must start small and work with the grain of what is. The path is never obvious. Examples:
  - The personal computer was first dismissed as a toy.
  - Instagram looks like photo filters, but helping people see the world through others' eyes is a step toward world peace, and it grew to over 200 million users in under four years.
- Don't be discouraged by people who dismiss your work as trivial because it isn't curing cancer or going to Mars. He quotes Feynman: "The worthwhile problems are the ones you can really solve or help solve, the ones you can really contribute something to." The patterns aim at an independent mind free of other people's limits, so you can judge for yourself what is worthwhile and act with conviction.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul argues that most good things in his life (Google, meeting his wife) came from unplanned events, not plans. He proposes "allowing" serendipity by removing its two main blocks: ego-fear and rigid plans. The fix is to hunt down fear, treat plans as flexible ideas, and respond to the unexpected with gratitude.

chunks.heading: Allowing serendipity instead of seeking or planning it
chunks.text:
Paul's theory: good things in his life (Google, his wife) came from low-key, unplanned actions that he let play out. He thinks in terms of "allowing" serendipity, not "seeking" or "creating" it. "Opportunity is all around us, but we have beliefs and habits that block it."

- His 11th-grade English teacher stopped for two soaked cross-country cyclists, took them home for dinner and heard their stories. Paul loved it because "none of it was planned -- they simply allowed it to happen." It felt like "the **fun** way to live."
- Google (1999): he sent his resume to a few companies he'd seen mentioned on Slashdot (he calls it a lazy job search, interested in startups and Linux). Most never responded; only Google offered a job. He was skeptical of its business and didn't expect it to last, but it "seemed like it could be fun and educational," so he accepted.
- His wife: soon after moving to California he signed up for match.com, read profiles, emailed three people, and one replied. He was not looking to marry.
- He notes most good things in his life "follow that general pattern, and aren't part of any 'plan'", and his plans rarely work unless they are "boringly simple."

chunks.heading: The two blocks to serendipity: ego-fear and "other plans"
chunks.text:
Paul names two main blockers of serendipity:

- **Ego-fear:** fear that goes beyond rational concern, driven by embarrassment, humiliation, rejection or criticism. It keeps people from public speaking, talking to strangers, interviewing for jobs.
- **"The plan":** attachment to one fixed plan.
- Healthy fear (not running onto a freeway) is different from ego-fear, but ego-fear "will rationalize itself as healthy fear," e.g. "I don't want to talk to that stranger because they could attack me, or waste my time."

chunks.heading: Ego-fear: how it costs opportunities and how to remove it
chunks.text:
- Example he cites: a Hacker News commenter who liked Google in 1999, applied for a sys admin/data center job, was called twice, and never called back because "they would not have hired me anyways." Paul calls that fear of rejection and humiliation, and says it probably blocks many great opportunities.
- Thinking your way out of it "only makes the problem worse by generating a more complex tangle of rationalizations." "Fear is defeated by confrontation -- avoidance only makes it stronger."
- He endorses Eleanor Roosevelt: "You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face. You must do the thing which you think you cannot do."
- His program: "seek ego-fear. Hunt it down and soak in it. Steal its energy." It is scary by definition, "That's good."

chunks.heading: Treat unexpected events with gratitude, not as obstacles
chunks.text:
- Serendipity and luck are unpredictable, so they don't fit any good plan. When something unexpected happens, people see a distraction or frustrating obstacle.
- "The difference between a life full of frustrating obstacles, and a life full of serendipity, is largely a matter of interpretation."
- His recommended response is gratitude: "Accept what is given." Even seemingly adverse events can lead to something great. He points to the film *Yes Man* as a cute caricature of this mindset.

chunks.heading: Have a thousand plans, not one
chunks.text:
