- He quotes Eisenhower: "Plans are worthless. Planning is essential." Planning isn't bad; obsessively sticking to a single plan leaves little room for serendipity.
- "The world is very complicated, and we humans are very stupid, so it's good to be flexible and open minded." His advice: "Instead of having one plan, have one thousand plans, and revise them as necessary."
- To avoid analysis paralysis (pouring energy into the perfect plan and never acting): pick a plan knowing it's flawed, set it in action, then adapt, revise or switch as the world unfolds.
- He calls plans "ideas" or "rough sketches" instead. He tries to avoid having plans for his life but has many ideas, and which happen "will be a surprise to me. It's more fun that way."

chunks.heading: Why predictability kills innovation
chunks.text:
- Paul suspects the desire for a definite plan is partly rooted in fear: uncertainty is scary, and a plan creates "the illusion of predictability in a very unpredictable world."
- Reducing risk and unpredictability also reduces serendipity.
- He sees this as a reason large organizations struggle to produce innovation: "they want it to be planned and scheduled, but that just kills it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buchheit argues that "more features = better" is the root of bad product design. Pick three or fewer attributes, get them very right, and treat the rest as noise. He uses the 2001 iPod and the original Gmail as examples, and says the advice applies mainly to consumer products.

chunks.heading: Pick three features and get them very right; everything else is noise
chunks.text:
- Paul argues the common product-design mistake is the "more features = better" mindset. It explains why "so many otherwise smart people are bad at product design (e.g. most open source projects)."
- Reviews of the 2001 iPod and the iPad focused on "missing" features. Those features usually exist in unsuccessful competitors, which leads people to wrongly conclude that a successful product needs even more features.
- His example: if a MacBook with OSX and no keyboard were the right product, Microsoft's tablet would have succeeded years earlier. "Copying the mistakes of a failed product isn't a great formula for success."
- His rule for new products: "Pick three key attributes or features, get those things very, very right, and then forget about everything else." Those three define the product's essence and value, and "the rest is noise."
- He asks founders: what are the three (or fewer) key features that make the product so great you can cut or half-ass everything else? Is at least 80% of your effort going into getting those right?

chunks.heading: The original iPod as a three-attribute product
chunks.text:
Paul's reading of the 2001 iPod:

1. Small enough to fit in your pocket.
2. Enough storage to hold many hours of music.
3. Easy to sync with your Mac. He guesses most hardware companies got this wrong because they can't make software.

- Everything else was absent: no wireless, no on-device playlist editing, no Ogg support.
- Slashdot's review dismissed it with "No wireless. Less space than a nomad. Lame."
- His point: the product was nothing but the essentials, well executed.

chunks.heading: How Gmail launched with a minimal feature set
chunks.text:
- Gmail's three core attributes at launch: it was fast, it stored all your email (when 4MB quotas were the norm), and it had an innovative interface built around conversations and search.
- Secondary and tertiary features were minimal or missing. There was no rich text composer.
- The original address book was built in two days and did almost nothing. The engineer wanted five days; Paul talked him down to two "since I never use that feature anyway."
- Those features can be added or improved later, and Gmail improved a lot after launch. But "if the basic product isn't compelling, adding more features won't save it."

chunks.heading: Why constraint reveals the product's true value
chunks.text:
- Focusing on a few core features in version one "forces you to find the true essence and value of the product."
- Test for innovation: if the product needs "everything" in order to be good, it's probably not very innovative. It might be a nice upgrade to an existing product, but not a new thing.
- His summary line: "if your product is great, it doesn't need to be good."

chunks.heading: Simplicity as a feature: the iPhone and iPad
chunks.text:
- Paul says he spends more time browsing the web on his iPhone than his laptop.
- Part of the reason is simplicity. The iPhone is ready in under half a second; the laptop takes at least a few seconds to wake and has distracting activity running.
- The iPhone feels like "a simple appliance that I use without a second thought." The laptop feels like a complex machine that makes him "pause and consider if it's worth the effort right now."
- The iPhone's downsides are small size and slowness, though he counts smallness as a feature too.
- He is unsure where the iPad ends up, and says making it succeed is Apple's problem. He expects its value to come from new behaviors enabled by "a fast, simple, and sharable internet window" sitting around the house.
- Examples he gives: casually browsing the web at home, sharing photos in person, board games (an idea from Bret), and at the office an easy way to chat with remote people while discussing a presentation or document, such as audio iChat with a shared display.
- These are theoretically possible on laptops, but they end up "so clumsy and complicated that we don't bother."

chunks.heading: When this advice does and doesn't apply
chunks.text:
- Paul says the advice probably applies only to consumer products, meaning ones where the purchaser is also the user. He includes some business products in that group.
- For markets with purchasing processes that have long feature-requirement lists, his advice is to "crank out as many features as possible and not waste time on simplicity or usability."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit argues every system has intended rules and actual rules, and the gap between them is where miracles happen. Important new businesses, like Google, are hacks that find gaps incumbents don't see or value. Building a company where others do the work is itself a big hack.

chunks.heading: Hacking as applied philosophy: finding the actual rules
chunks.text:
Paul defines hacking as applied philosophy. Every system has two sets of rules: the rules as intended or commonly perceived, and the actual rules ("reality"). In most complex systems the gap between them is huge. Once someone discovers the actual rules, it becomes possible to perform "miracles", meaning things that violate the perceived rules.

- Paul calls the discovery of actual rules the core of hacking.
- Computer hackers do this literally: they find the actual rules of a system (his example is buffer overflows) and use them to circumvent the intended rules (typically access controls). The same applies to people who break DRM.
- He thinks the common use of "hacker" for people who subvert computer systems is "essentially correct", even though the term is occasionally disputed.

chunks.heading: Hacking in code: elegant hacks and ugly hacks
chunks.text:
Paul also uses "hacking" for writing clever or ugly code, where the hacker violates expectations of how software gets written.

- A project that should take months but gets hacked out in a single evening is "a small miracle, and a major hack".
- If the result is simple and beautiful because the hacker found a better solution, it is an "elegant" or "brilliant" hack.
- If the result is complex and hard to understand (for example, it violates many layers of abstraction), it is an "ugly hack".
- Ugly hacks are not all bad. One of his favorite personal hacks was messy code that demonstrated what would become AdSense. The code was quickly discarded, but "it did its job". He tells that story in his post "Communicating with code".

chunks.heading: Hacking applies to every system, not just computers
chunks.text:
Paul argues that our entire reality is "systems of systems, all the way down", so wherever there are systems there is potential for hacking. His examples:

- Human relations: *The Game*, an account of people hacking human attraction.
- Health: Seth Roberts's ideas.
- Sports: Tim Ferriss's claim to have hacked the National Chinese Kickboxing championship.
- Finance: "too big to fail".

chunks.heading: "There are always shortcuts and loopholes"
chunks.text:
Against the common advice that there are no shortcuts to success and that it is all hard work and doing what you're told, Paul says the hacking mindset takes the opposite approach: "**There are always shortcuts and loopholes**."

- Hacking is sometimes perceived as cheating or unfair, and it can be. Using social hacks to steal billions is wrong (he cites Madoff).
- Automation is his example of a good hack. Getting machines to do our work enabled a much higher standard of living, even though not everyone saw it that way (the Luddites were not fans).

chunks.heading: Important new businesses are usually hacks
chunks.text:
Paul says important new businesses are usually some kind of hack. Established businesses think they understand the system and set up rules to guard their profits and prevent real competition. A new business must find a gap in those rules: something the incumbents either don't see or don't consider important.

Google is his example. The existing search engines thought of themselves as portals and believed two things:
- Search quality wasn't very important, because regular people can't tell the difference.
- Search wasn't very valuable anyway, because it sends people away from your site.

Google's success came in large part from recognizing that others were wrong on both points.

chunks.heading: Building wealth is itself a hack
chunks.text:
Paul argues that the entire process of building a business and having other people and computers do the work for you is a big hack.

- "Nobody ever created a billion dollars through direct physical labor." Creating that much wealth requires major shortcuts, and by definition those shortcuts were mostly invisible to others (though many will dispute that after the fact).
- Startup investing takes the hack to the next level by having other people do the work of building the business. He notes that finding the right people and businesses is not easy.

chunks.heading: The hacker mindset creates the future
chunks.text:
Paul says not everyone has the hacker mindset and that society needs a variety of personalities. But wherever there were people, there was someone "staring into the system, searching for the truth".

- Some people are content to find a truth. Others use their discoveries to hack the system and transform the world.
- Those people created the governments, businesses, religions and other machines that operate society, and they necessarily did it by hacking the prior systems. Incumbents don't give up easily, as anyone trying to establish a new government or religion would find.
- To discover great hacks, we must keep searching for the true nature of reality while acknowledging that we do not currently possess the truth and never will.
- His conclusion: hacking is much bigger than clever bits of code. "It's how we create the future."
- He closes with humility: "Or at least that's how I see it. Maybe I'll change my mind later."
- He points readers to "The Knack" and the need to disassemble things.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit uses Gmail's history (disliked for years, doomed in many insiders' eyes, then growing 40% in a year) to argue that important products take years to succeed. The right response is to move very fast and stay frugal so you survive the long climb, while treating user complaints as a sign people care.

chunks.heading: Gmail's long road: why "overnight success" is misleading
chunks.text:
Paul uses Gmail's history to argue that big products take years, and that early disbelief is normal.

- Work on Gmail began in August or September 2001. It launched on April 1, 2004, about two and a half years later.
- For a long time almost everyone disliked it. Some people used it anyway because of the search, but "they had endless complaints."
- Quite a few people wanted to kill it or "reboot" it as an enterprise product with native client software, "not this crazy Javascript stuff."
- Even at launch, many people inside Google predicted doom: the product was too weird and nobody wants to change email services. He was told Gmail would never get a million users.
- After launch it was still called "niche" and "not used by real people outside of silicon valley."
- Almost 7.5 years after starting, a Financial Times piece (cited by Paul) put Gmail at close to 100m users worldwide, versus more than 250m each for Yahoo and Microsoft webmail (comScore). In the US, Gmail users grew more than 40% in the past year, versus 2% for Yahoo and a 7% fall for Microsoft.
- He notes that count likely excludes "Apps for your domain" users, and that he "still [has] a huge list of complaints about Gmail."

chunks.heading: Big success takes years, with few counter-examples
chunks.text:
- Paul's expectation: "big success takes years, and there aren't many counter-examples."
- YouTube is the one fast exception he names, and it hadn't yet reached piles of money.
- Facebook grew very fast but was almost 5 years old at the time.
- Larry and Sergey started Google in 1996. When Paul joined in 1999, few people had heard of it.
- He calls the notion of overnight success "very misleading, and rather harmful."

chunks.heading: What to do if you're starting something new
chunks.text:
- Expect a long journey.
- That is no excuse to move slow. "You must move very fast, otherwise you will never arrive, because it's a long journey!"
- Be frugal, so you don't "starve to death half the way up the mountain."

chunks.heading: Don't overgeneralize from your own success
chunks.text:
- Paul warns against assuming that because Gmail took off, FriendFeed will too. The products are very different, and "maybe we just got lucky with Gmail."
- The Gmail story only gives perspective: creating an important new product generally takes time, and the product has to keep changing and improving. He points to old Gmail screenshots as proof of how rough it once was.
- FriendFeed (at the time) "shows a lot of promise, but it's still a 'work in progress.'"

chunks.heading: Complaints mean people care; launch early to get them
chunks.text:
- Paul is always concerned by complaints about a service, but also encouraged: people write long blog posts about what to change because they care about the product.
- That attention suggests the product is "at least headed in roughly the right direction."
- Silence would worry him more: it would mean nobody cares and the team is "off in the weeds."
- He calls this feedback "one of the major benefits of launching early."
- He expects the product to need to evolve, since "our product isn't quite right."

chunks.heading: Asking users to describe their ideal product
chunks.text:
- Paul invites users to write up their vision of "the perfect FriendFeed" for themselves, on their own blog (or via a Posterous email address if they have none).
- They are free to drop or change features.
- He admits they are "technically... doing my work for me," but frames it as mutually beneficial: the team will try to build something users like, and even if not, others can use the concepts since they are public.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A personal essay written on the eighth anniversary of his brother's death, after Gmail's launch and his daughter's premature birth. It contains no tactical advice on growth or marketing, but states a mindset on acceptance, being good to yourself and others, and doing work for its own sake rather than for future reward.

chunks.heading: Accepting a hard present by accepting the past
chunks.text:
Paul describes a practice he began while his daughter was in the hospital: "Accept. Accept. Accept." He applies it to everything, including a slow driver in traffic. His reasoning is "I can't even see the other timelines, maybe this one is somehow better."

- Repetition is the key to the practice: every day, every moment.
- Small annoyances (traffic) give him daily reps for the larger things (a baby who may not survive).
- He concludes that to be at peace with the present, we must be at peace with the past, because "the present is a product of the past."
- "What happened, happened." Learn to love the present moment.

chunks.heading: Trusting that the pieces fit without bargaining for meaning
chunks.text:
Paul says he keeps looking for meaning in loss and has found little beyond acceptance. He notes that our lives are "mere brush strokes on the canvas of reality," so the big picture is hard to see.

- Trusting that it all fits together into something beautiful is, in his words, "the purest form of faith."
- Anything else is "a dangerous distraction."
- No contracts with God, no expectations of reward, "just trust."
- He admits that life is unfair: his brother Steve died of pancreatic cancer at 33, three months after diagnosis, and weeks later Gmail launched and that summer Google went public.

chunks.heading: Work as a place to focus the mind during grief
chunks.text:
After his brother's funeral in March 2004, Paul went back to work. He says it can be wonderful to focus on something simple that he can control, like computers.

- Gmail launched a few weeks after Steve died (2004).
- Google's IPO followed that summer.
- Paul's point is that building can be a refuge, while also being a reminder that success and fairness are unrelated ("Life is unfair. Very unfair.").

chunks.heading: Startups and money are games; being good to people is the point
chunks.text:
Paul worries that when he writes about startups and other interests, he may be communicating the wrong priorities.

- Investing money and creating new products "are wonderful games and can be a lot of fun, but it's important to remember that it's all just a game."
- What matters most is being good to each other and to ourselves.
- He argues you can't do only one: "we must do both or neither."
- "If we 'win', but have failed to do that, then we have lost. Winning is nothing."

chunks.heading: Push hard for its own sake, not for a future reward
chunks.text:
Paul says pushing yourself and stretching your limits is healthy, but only when done for its own sake.

- The people who learn to love what they do are the ones who accomplish the most anyway.
- Those who push only for a future reward, or to avoid failure, "very often burn out, sometimes tragically."
- His direct plea: "Please don't do that."
- He closes with: "Please be good to each other, and your self."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit reviews his first three years of angel investing (2006-2008: about $1.21M across 32 companies). He shares real results, why he invests, and two core rules: assume you'll lose your money and invest in many companies. He also explains why Y Combinator companies delivered his best returns.

chunks.heading: Angel investing results: 32 companies, ~10% gain in 3 years
chunks.text: Paul started angel investing in 2006 assuming he didn't know what he was doing. His stated goals were to learn through experience, help startups, and not lose too much money. He has no single investing criterion: sometimes the idea looks good, sometimes the people, sometimes he's just curious what will happen. In every case he wants to be helpful and learn something.

chunks.heading: The numbers from 2006-2008 investments
chunks.text:
- Invested about $1.21 million across 32 companies (2006 to 2008).
- About half were acquired or are dead/mostly dead. The other half are alive and seem to be doing well.
- The acquisitions to date total about $1.34 million, roughly a 10% gain. He calls it "not great, but at least I'm not losing too much."
- Only two companies are officially dead, with at least four "zombies" that exist in minimal form and are almost certainly worthless.
- Acquisitions by other private companies (for example ScanScout, bought by Tremor Media) count as "still alive and doing well", since they gave investors no liquidity.
- He expects the final return to be much better than 10% because the surviving group includes promising companies such as Meraki, Weebly and Wufoo. He treats any return as "gravy" since his primary goal was learning and being helpful.

chunks.heading: Exits: where the returns came from
chunks.text:
- Only two exits returned more than 10x: Heroku (reported $212M sale to Salesforce) and Mint (reported $170M sale to Intuit).
- Both were among his smaller checks. He says this shows he doesn't know what he's doing, or at least that he needs to put more money into the best companies.
- Mint was oversubscribed. He didn't remember why he put less into Heroku, then edited the post to note it was also oversubscribed.
- Medium exits: AppJet/Etherpad (Google) and 280North (Motorola, reported $20M).
- Smaller but still good 2x-3x exits: Auctomatic, Parakey (Facebook) and Zenter (Google).
- On criticism of these small deals: "as much as I'd like to get a nice 10,000x exit, I'm certainly not going to complain when someone doubles my money!"

chunks.heading: Why he keeps investing in Y Combinator companies
chunks.text:
- His highest return came from a YC company (Heroku, winter 2008). He had invested in YC companies almost from the start (Wufoo, winter 2006), and says they keep getting better.
- He argues YC attracts the best founders, and Heroku is "just the tip of the iceberg."
- It compounds: the more great YC companies there are, the more reasons other smart founders have to join. He finds himself asking non-YC companies why they aren't in YC yet.
- This trend contributed to his decision to join YC as a partner (announced November 2010, alongside Harj Taggar).

chunks.heading: His advice for new angel investors
chunks.text:
- **Assume you'll lose your money.**
- **Plan on investing in a large number of companies.**
- Attend YC demo day (his third piece of advice).
- Have the right motivations (helping startups and learning to be a better investor) and the right expectations. Anyone planning to find the next Google, invest a bunch, and get super-rich "is going to be very disappointed."
- He says his own results validate this advice. He jokes that his current billion-dollar plan is finding the next Google and buying a 1% stake.

chunks.heading: Lessons he draws about his own investing
chunks.text:
- Learning by doing is the only way he sees to get better, so he invested broadly across a variety of startups.
- Returns are concentrated in a very few winners, so the biggest lesson is to size up the best companies instead of spreading checks evenly.
- Oversubscribed rounds can limit how much a good investor gets to put in, which is part of why the biggest winners were small checks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buchheit argues that attachment to identity and false standards breeds fear and insecurity that cloud our judgment. By dropping ego ("I am nothing"), you can see things as they are, accept and understand problems, and improve genuinely rather than hiding or faking. Useful as a mindset for founders and builders.

chunks.heading: "I am nothing": dropping identity to see clearly
chunks.text:
Paul argues that the roles and labels people hold (good employee, good man or woman, smart, rational, introvert, winner, expert) are false standards and false dichotomies. They are so ingrained that people believe them without noticing.

- Nobody measures up to these standards, "and nobody should."
- People hide insecurities and compare themselves to peers, so everyone sees others as having it figured out and "nobody can see the truth anymore."
- Rebelling by being a "bad whatever" is still control by the same false standard: "they are still not being themselves."
- He calls this comparison-and-pretending path "insanity," and "all so exhausting."

chunks.heading: "I am nothing": the core move
chunks.text:
Paul's answer is to hold no identity, so there is nothing to defend. Every identity carries a matching fear:

- Smart: afraid of looking stupid.
- Successful: afraid of failure.
- Expert: afraid of being wrong.
- Rational: afraid of emotions.
- Introverted: afraid of meeting new people.
- Respectable: afraid of looking foolish.

His conclusion: "But I am nothing, and so I am finally free to be myself."

This is not a license to stagnate. He says change is inevitable, and "if we aren't changing for the better, then we are just slowly decaying."

chunks.heading: Zero expectations make it possible to see what is true
chunks.text:
Paul says fear, jealousy, insecurity, unfairness and embarrassment cloud our ability to see "what is." Once defenses are up, it is hard to be honest with anyone, "even ourselves."

- With no image, identity or ego to protect, he can see and accept things as they really are.
- That is "the beginning of positive change, because we can not change what we do not accept and do not understand."
- Understanding lets you tell fixing problems from hiding them, and genuine improvement from faking it.
- "Many of our weaknesses are actually strengths once we learn how to use them, and... our greatest gifts are often buried beneath our greatest insecurities."

chunks.heading: Use emotions as a cue, not a verdict
chunks.text:
Paul says there is "no such thing as a bad emotion, just bad responses to emotions." Pride, anger, fear, jealousy, insecurity, unfairness, embarrassment and bitterness can all be useful.

His method:

1. Notice the emotion.
2. Use it as a cue to remember "I am nothing" and let go of identity.
3. Ask why you feel it. It is typically because something has threatened your identity.
4. Treat it as a pointer to the buried truth.

His example of a bad response: the "torturing children" case (a documented anti-effeminacy experiment) as a harmful reaction to fears about one's own sexuality.

chunks.heading: Self-improvement: direction matters, comparison doesn't
chunks.text:
- Letting go of identity "can be difficult and takes time, possibly forever."
- "Moving in the right direction is all that really matters."
- Don't compare yourself with others, because "you didn't start in the same place or with the same challenges."
- Real improvement means "becoming a better version of our selves, not a lesser version of someone else."
- Without self-acceptance and understanding, you can't know what a better version looks like or whether you're headed the right way.
- His analogy: it would be like "putting the final touches on the Mona Lisa while picturing some celebrity you saw on the cover of People magazine -- the result would be a mess."
- The process is peeling off "the shell of false identity that prevents our true self from growing." His closing line: "And it starts with nothing."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A personal essay in which Paul Buchheit describes how his brother's death and his daughter's premature birth taught him to ask whether he is spending his life well. It offers a mindset framework (people matter, everything else is noise) rather than tactical business advice.

chunks.heading: Paul's framing: death as clarity, and the question he asks himself
chunks.text:
- After his brother Steve died (Steve was 33, Paul was 27), Paul says he understood death "at a visceral level" for the first time, not just intellectually.
- He found "live every day as though it's your last" impractical, so he reframed it as a question: "Is this how I want to spend the rest of my life?"
- He first asked what he would do with six years left. At first he thought the answer was an audacious goal like curing cancer. Over time he concluded it simply meant being mindful of how he lives.
- The answers can be surprising. Cleaning the kitchen is relaxing and makes a pleasant, healthy space for family and friends. Sitting in a windowless conference room while people he doesn't love debate things he doesn't care about is not how he wants to spend his life.
- He stresses this is personal: others may find real meaning in what he doesn't.
- His summary: "Death strips away everything that doesn't matter... People matter. Everything else is noise."

chunks.heading: Using mortality as a filter for how to spend time
chunks.text:
- Paul treats the question as a recurring check on daily activities, not a one-time life plan.
- It filters out low-meaning work: meetings and debates with people and topics he doesn't care about.
- It favors small acts that serve the people around him (a clean kitchen as a gathering place).
- He admits he struggles to retain this: "Life gets busy, and I forget what matters." The reminders are all around us "if only we can open our eyes."

chunks.heading: Presence and unconditional love, learned from his premature daughter
chunks.text:
- His daughter was born 100 days early, weighing 1 pound 10 ounces, on a ventilator, eyelids still fused, during a trip in northern New Mexico. His wife April was airlifted to Albuquerque; he drove several hours alone overnight.
- Doctors couldn't say if she would survive. Each visit might be the last, so he lived "every day as though it might be her last."
- Complications followed: brain bleeding, hydrocephalus requiring brain surgery, a flight to San Francisco (no pediatric neurosurgeons in New Mexico), more surgeries, meningitis, and a stop in breathing.
- His coping method: the future was too terrifying and the past a reminder of loss, but "most moments, on their own, were ok." He focused on holding his baby, appreciating each moment, and loving her unconditionally.
- Practical takeaway he draws: when everything is uncertain, all you have is now. You can love and expect nothing in return.
- Outcome: she is now a healthy seven-year-old (as of 2012).

chunks.heading: Finding the gift in tragedy
chunks.text:
- His thesis: "In every tragedy, there is a gift, if we are able to see and accept it."
- From his brother: a personal understanding of death and a constant reminder to live as though life may end at any moment.
- From his daughter: what unconditional love means, loving without expecting anything in return.
- He acknowledges the gifts "were delivered at great cost."
- When life is "smashed to bits," people look for a North Star. His is unconditional love, which he wants to feel at a visceral level, not just understand intellectually.

chunks.heading: The fable: God of Unconditional Love vs. the Devil's false gods
chunks.text:
- Paul wrote a simple story because stories engage the imagination and make abstract concepts "come alive inside of us." He says you don't need to believe in anything supernatural to get it.
- The setup: the Devil boasted he could gather more followers than God. God's method was simple: give everyone Unconditional Love and Forgiveness, "nothing more and nothing less."
- The Devil's plan: lie that he is the One True God, promise a great afterlife reward, and threaten hell for non-followers. He bet that Greed and Fear are stronger than Love and could trick even good people.
- His test for a false God (or false image of God):
  - Promises a reward (such as 72 virgins) for violence, such as flying a plane into a building.
  - Threatens hell for loving the wrong person.
  - Tells you to coerce others into worshiping.
  - Promises protection in exchange for doing his bidding.
- Principle: the God of Unconditional Love "brings union through love"; false gods "bring division through fear and greed."
- Genuine love "must be freely given and freely accepted, with nothing expected in return." It can't be delivered "at gun point, or with the threat of eternal damnation."
- His closing call: give unconditional love and forgiveness to others and, most urgently, to ourselves.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit argues most people judge risk by the most likely outcome, so they ignore downside and feel cheated when it hits. He instead looks at the worst case (~0.01 percentile) and the best case (~95th), and takes the gamble if he is comfortable with the downside and excited by the upside, using a few heuristics to raise expected value.

chunks.heading: Assume the startup fails: judge decisions by the worst case and the best case, not the likely case
chunks.text:
Paul argues most people ask "What is the most likely outcome?" and proceed if it looks good. That works for "normal" decisions like school, a job or a house. It also makes people ignore bad outcomes, so they feel bitter or cheated when one hits. His examples: "I have a degree, now where's my job!?", and house buyers who never considered that a new house could lose 20% of its value and leave them owing more than it was worth.

When advising on startups, he tells people to start from the assumption that the startup will fail and all their equity will become worthless. Many people say they couldn't stay motivated believing that. Paul finds it unfortunate that they feel they must lie to themselves to stay motivated, and he realized he simply uses a different method of evaluating risk.

chunks.heading: The two questions Paul asks: "What's the worst that could happen?" and "Could it be awesome?"
chunks.text:
- Instead of the median outcome, he looks at roughly the 0.01 percentile and the 95th percentile outcomes.
- For a startup, the worst case is usually losing your entire investment (but learning a lot).
- The best case is making a large pile of money, creating something cool, and learning a lot.
- Thinking about the best case is easy and common, which is partly why it gets disrespected ("dreamer" isn't usually a compliment).
- The mistake is ignoring the worst case because thinking about bad things is uncomfortable. He links this to people killing themselves over investment losses, partly because they were not planning for the worst case.

chunks.heading: Why planning for the worst case is also an emotional buffer
chunks.text:
- Thinking about the worst case protects you from dumb mistakes.
- It also provides an emotional buffer: "If I'm comfortable with the worst-case outcome, then I can move without fear and focus my attention on the opportunity."
- Caveat: when considering the worst case, count the impact on others. Even if you're fine with dying, that outcome may cause unacceptable harm to people in your life.

chunks.heading: Heuristics that raise a bet's expected value
chunks.text:
Best and worst case alone is imperfect. Lottery tickets have an acceptable worst case (you lose $1) and a great best case (millions), yet are generally a bad deal. Paul says to use expected value when it's available (as with lottery tickets, so don't buy them). For most real decisions it isn't, because "the world is too complicated and math is hard", so he uses heuristics:

- Will I learn a lot from the experience? (failure can be very educational)
- Will it make my life more interesting? ("a predictable life is a boring life")
- Is it good for the world? (even if he doesn't benefit, maybe someone else will)

If these are mostly true, he is excited about the best case and comfortable with the worst case, it's "probably a good gamble."

chunks.heading: Which risks to ignore: why he picks the 0.01 percentile
chunks.text:
- In the year he wrote this, the US had 37,261 motor vehicle fatalities in a population of 304,059,724, so his odds of dying in a car accident are very roughly 1/10,000 per year.
- He notes many of those deaths involved teenagers and alcoholics, so his own odds are probably a little better, but it's good as a rough estimate.
- Using this logic, he treats 1/10,000 as the cutoff for the worst case worth planning around, and largely ignores obscure 1/1,000,000 risks, which are too numerous and difficult to protect against anyway.

chunks.heading: Cynical optimist
chunks.text: Paul has been called both extremely cynical and unreasonably optimistic. He is fine being a "cynical optimist": cynical about the downside, optimistic about the upside. He points to related essays: "Why I'd rather be wrong" and "The other half of the story".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit explains why working prototypes beat speeches and slide decks. Using Gmail and the origin of AdSense for content, he shows how shipping rough code to real users settles arguments, and why products need cheap ways (labs, 20% time, public APIs) for people to experiment.

chunks.heading: Prototype instead of pitching
chunks.text:
- Paul distrusts ideas sold through "brilliant speeches" and "slick powerpoints", partly because it's easy to overlook messy details or get caught up in details that seem important but aren't. He also gets bored by endless debate, and says he is bad at selling ideas that way.
- His alternative is to build the thing and watch the response: "Your code can be a very persuasive argument."
- He advises spending less time talking and more time prototyping, especially for people who aren't good at talking or slides.
- With a live prototype he didn't need to sell anyone. He wrote the code, released the feature and watched the reaction.

chunks.heading: Always have live code: how Gmail was built
chunks.text:
- The first version of Gmail was written in a day. He took the Google Groups (Usenet search) code from his previous project and stuffed his own email into it. It only searched his mail, but it was live and people could use it.
- From that day until launch, every new feature went live immediately and most new ideas were implemented as soon as possible.
- This caused a lot of churn: the frontend was rewritten about six times and the backend three times before launch. The payoff was direct experience with every feature.
- Features that seemed like great ideas often failed once tried. Things expected to be big problems or very confusing turned out fine, and the team forgot the theoretical problems once they were in.
- Usually everyone, including Paul, ended up hating whatever was released (especially his own ideas). They always learned something and could move on to other ideas quickly.
- He lists this as one thing done "very right" in 2.5 years of pre-launch development, in which "we did a lot of things wrong."

chunks.heading: Content-targeted ads (AdSense): a bad idea proved by a few-hours prototype
chunks.text:
- Targeting keyword ads to arbitrary web content had floated around Google for a long time. It was "obvious" but also "obviously bad": most people thought it needed fancy AI to understand content, and that nobody would click the ads. Paul thought they were probably right.
- Gmail needed a way to make money, and Sanjeev Singh kept pushing relevant ads. Paul was skeptical but thought it might be a fun experiment.
- How he built it, in a few hours:
  - Connected to the ads database, copied out all ads and keywords, and did light sorting and filtering with unix shell commands.
  - Hacked the "adult content" classifier he and Matt Cutts had written for safe-search. It was a separate code branch, so breaking its original function didn't matter.
  - Changed it to classify pages by which ad was most relevant, then loaded the ads data into it.
  - Linked it into the Gmail prototype UI and showed the ad in a small box.
- The code was "ugly and hackish". He released it to about 100 Googlers and went to sleep.
- The reaction the next day was negative; someone may have used the word "blasphemous". But the ads were amusing and often relevant. A lost-sunglasses email got a sunglasses ad, and a lunch menu got a balsamic vinegar ad.
- Others also found the ads surprisingly relevant. Content-targeted ads went from a lowest-priority, unstaffed project to a top priority. An "extremely talented team" was formed and a live beta shipped in roughly six months.
- It became a business with "billions of dollars in revenue (I think)". None of his prototype code reached the real product, but it showed the idea had real potential, which his arguments could not.

chunks.heading: Keep prototyping cheap as the product grows
chunks.text:
- Making it fast and easy to prototype new ideas, especially bad ones, is important, and gets harder as a product scales.
- Contrast: stuffing random broken features into Gmail was easy with about 100 users who all worked at Google, but "not so simple when there are 100 million users."
- Gmail's solution: Gmail Labs, which lets thousands of Google engineers add new UI features.
- Google's "20% time" works for the same reason. For innovation, people must be able to work on ideas that are unapproved and generally thought to be stupid. The real value of 20% is "not the time, but rather the 'license' it gives to work on things that 'aren't important'."

chunks.heading: Public APIs let outsiders prototype for you
chunks.text:
- Paul calls an API one of the best ways to enable prototyping and innovation on an established product.
- Twitter is his example: thousands of third-party clients, new ones written daily, and he believes a majority of Twitter messages come in through them.
- Reasoning: "no matter how brilliant you and your coworkers are, there are always going to be smarter people outside of your company."

chunks.heading: Use your API to find and hire builders
chunks.text:
- At FriendFeed, the API did more than enable apps; it revealed great app developers.
- Gary Burd and Benjamin Golub were both writing FriendFeed apps with the API before FriendFeed hired them.
- Hiring takeaway: you don't have to guess who is "smart and gets things done"; you can watch it in the wild.

chunks.heading: Example: a FriendFeed prototype built in the browser
chunks.text:
- Paul found it hard to judge an idea from words or mockups: "I really need to try it out." So he built a prototype of his "ideal FriendFeed" in his spare time.
- It is a single web page, a few hundred lines of HTML and JS, running entirely in the browser and fetching data from FriendFeed's JSON APIs. No server is needed, so others can copy and modify it easily.
- Ideas he tried:
  - Treat entries, comments and likes all as simple "messages".
  - Show only comments from the user's friends (which can be a little confusing).
  - Put everything in reverse-chronological order.
- He stresses it isn't "the future of FriendFeed", just a collection of ideas, some he likes and some he doesn't.
- He invited others to copy the code and build their own prototypes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul argues the biggest startup failure mode is building something nobody wants, no matter how brilliant the team or technology. The fix is humility: pay attention to what works, ship early, iterate on user feedback, and "find the gradient, then follow it." He illustrates with Gmail, FriendFeed, MySpace and YouTube.

chunks.heading: Product-market fit matters more than team, tech, or design
chunks.text:
Paul Buchheit agrees with Marc Andreessen that market is the most important factor in a startup's success. Andreessen's argument: in a great market, "the market pulls product out of the startup." The first viable product wins, and the product only has to "basically work." Paul's version of the point is that a product nobody wants is not a great product, and a team that keeps building something nobody wants is not a great team.

He draws two lessons from it:
- **Even the best people fail if people don't want the product.** The smartest, most experienced, best-connected team can build the most stunningly designed and technically advanced product and still fail. His example is the Segway.
- **Ordinary people can win by building the right product.** A team that isn't the smartest, with a product that is "kind of ugly and broken," can still be very successful. His examples are YouTube and MySpace.

chunks.heading: Why strong teams build the wrong product: overrating their own skills
chunks.text:
Paul says good teams fail because of attitude. They overestimate how much their own skills matter:
- Engineers think success is about fancy technology and complex engineering (he adds "hello Google").
- Designers think it is about beautiful design.
- MBAs think it is about knowing the right people, or spreadsheets.

He says especially smart or successful teams can be worse. They tend to be arrogant and overconfident, so they question their assumptions less.

His examples of the wrong attitude:
- When Google acquired YouTube, many people inside Google were flabbergasted: "But they have no technology!?" Paul's reply: you only need enough technology to make the product work, and any more means you probably have the wrong priorities.
- Similar complaints get aimed at Facebook, MySpace and other popular sites. People say MySpace or even Google has "no design" or "bad design". Paul says they have enough design, or the right design, for their users.

chunks.heading: The right attitude is humility: pay attention and iterate
chunks.text:
Paul's answer to the wrong attitude is humility. However smart, successful and qualified you are, "you simply don't know what you're doing." Nobody else does either, though some are foolish enough to think they do, and that is why you can beat them.

His humble approach to product design:
- Pay attention. Notice which things are working and which aren't.
- Experiment and iterate.
- Question your assumptions, and remember you are wrong about a lot of things.
- Watch for the signals.
- Lose your technical and design snobbery. "Whatever works, works."

chunks.heading: MySpace custom profiles: noticing an accident and keeping it
chunks.text:
Paul uses MySpace's custom profile layouts as his example of paying attention. He is "pretty sure" they were an accident:
- MySpace didn't properly escape the text users put on their profiles.
- That let users include arbitrary HTML and CSS in their pages.
- This is a common bug. Most teams would have fixed it and moved on, and really great engineers wouldn't have had the bug at all.
- MySpace instead noticed the feature was popular and found a way to preserve it.
- The result is mostly ugly but extremely popular.

He says "accidental" isn't the same as "random". There are clues all around, and you need to watch more closely to catch them.

chunks.heading: Release early and iterate: how Gmail started
chunks.text:
For web products, Paul calls release early and iterate a "very powerful technique." The sooner you test ideas, the sooner you can fix them.

His account of Gmail:
- He wrote the first version in one day, and it was not very impressive. He stuffed his own email into the Google Groups (Usenet) indexing engine.
- He sent it to a few people. They said it was somewhat useful but would be better searching their email instead of his. That was version two.
- After that release, people wanted to respond to email too. That was version three.
- That loop ran for a couple of years inside Google before the public release.

chunks.heading: Startups must launch much sooner than Gmail did, as with FriendFeed
chunks.text:
Gmail could iterate privately because Google had hundreds of internal users. Startups don't, so Paul says they need to release to the world much sooner.

His FriendFeed example:
- The product was semi-released (private beta) in October 2007, when it was only about two months old.
- It was 99.9% written by two people, Bret and Jim.
- Paul says the product by February 2008 was much better than what they would have built without launching, because "we have users, and we listen to them, and we see which things work and which don't."

His summary line: "Find the gradient, then follow it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Buchheit argues both "ideas are worthless" and "ideas are valuable" are wrong when stated simply. Using a mountain-climbing metaphor, he shows that value comes from the judgment to pick the right product and route, plus a team able to execute, and that ideas gain value when they come from someone with a track record of being right.

chunks.heading: Ideas are neither worthless nor valuable on their own
chunks.text:
- Paul notes two camps. Normal people assume ideas are worth millions (the Pet Rock). Engineers, VCs and successful entrepreneurs say ideas are worthless, and Paul Graham offers a "proof": there is no market for startup ideas, so there is no demand.
- Paul has "ideas all of the time, many more than I have time for", so he leans toward "worthless". He still sees a "nagging inconsistency" in that view.
- The inconsistency: Marc Andreessen argues market is the most important factor, so a mediocre team building the right product succeeds and a brilliant team building the wrong product fails. Paul says that is a lot like saying the right idea does matter, and asks why great teams execute perfectly on bad ideas.
- His conclusion: both camps are wrong "when stated so simply".

chunks.heading: The mountain metaphor: products are mountains with gold at some summits
chunks.text:
- Paul says to imagine products as mountains. To build a product you climb the mountain.
- Some mountains have a big pot of gold at the top and some do not. To make money you must pick the right mountain and also climb to the top and gather the gold.
- There are two ways to fail: choosing a mountain with little or no gold, or dying on the way up.
- Many mountains have never been climbed. Others were attempted and abandoned: the team froze, or there was no gold when they arrived.
- Mount Everest has fifteen recognized routes (per Wikipedia), some easier than others, so the route matters as well as the mountain.

chunks.heading: Judgment is the underrated half of execution
chunks.text:
- Paul says judgment "isn't talked about as much as execution, but it's obviously very important".
- Climbing needs a level of technical ability that depends on the mountain and route. It also needs judgment to choose the right route, and to change course when the current path isn't working.
- His example: a technically brilliant team hits a sheer cliff and thinks, "this is the perfect opportunity to use Erlang!" (he calls Erlang just a funny example of fancy tech). A team with better judgment sees an easier route around the other side.
- Judgment also drives which mountain to climb, since the landscape holds millions of them.

chunks.heading: Why the people selling ideas get brushed off
chunks.text:
- Paul pictures people wandering the flatlands near the mountains. They have ideas about which mountains hold gold, and some have drawn crude maps of an "easy" route.
- They try to sell the ideas and maps to climbers, and the climbers brush them off as worthless.
- When a team finds a huge cache of gold, the idea-sellers say, "I had that idea first! They stole my idea!"
- Paul grants they did have the idea, as did many other people. "Ideas are plentiful. The problem is that most ideas are bad": either there's no gold at the top, or the ascent is too hard with today's technology.
- What's valuable is "the judgment to know which mountains have the gold, and the team that can get to it".

chunks.heading: When an idea does have value: the track record of whoever holds it
chunks.text:
- If a skilled climber who has chosen the right mountains before thinks he knows where another gold-rich mountain is, people will listen. The idea has value because it comes from someone "who has a history of being right".
- The identical idea from a random person with no experience and no ability to execute will probably be ignored, because there's not enough evidence it's good.
- That person, if they truly believe in it, has to prove it on their own. Paul calls this "the beauty of our system": they often can, even if everyone else thinks it's a bad idea.
- A person with a history of being right plus a capable team that has shown technical skill and judgment on other mountains is "very valuable" and will have no trouble getting an idea funded.

chunks.heading: Paul's formula
chunks.text:
- Summary: Idea * Judgment * Ability * Determination * Luck = $$$
- It is a product of terms, so a weak factor drags the whole result down. Ideas are one input, not the whole thing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit splits product ideas into three types and argues the real low-hanging fruit sits in the "bad ideas" category, because good and bad ideas are nearly indistinguishable up front. His takeaways: test ideas faster and cheaper instead of debating them, and remember an idea is worthless until you build a real product.

chunks.heading: Obvious ideas split into two groups that are hard or overhyped
chunks.text:
Paul divides product ideas into three categories. The first two are the "obviously good" ones.

- **Category 1:** obviously good ideas that are very difficult to implement. Examples: efficient cold fusion, flying cars, other sci-fi ideas.
- **Category 2:** obviously "good" ideas that seem possible but haven't happened yet. Examples: video phones and HDTV for a long time.
- He thinks category 2 happens when people get excited about technology and overestimate the benefits (and possibly underestimate the cost). On video phones: "I just don't care that much about having a video phone."
- Category 1 only makes sense for a "super-genius researcher" dedicating a life to a really important problem they may never solve.
- Category 2 only makes sense if you find a clever way to dramatically cut implementation cost, as Skype did for the video phone.

chunks.heading: Category 3: "bad" ideas are indistinguishable from great ones in advance
chunks.text:
- Category 3 is "bad" ideas. Many are truly bad, but some turn out in hindsight to have been very good, and the two are hard to tell apart without hindsight.
- Examples he gives of ideas that looked bad:
  - The personal computer: "why would anyone need a computer?"
  - Google: "there are already too many search engines, and besides, search engines don't make money."
  - Blogger: "can't you just use Geocities, and besides, are there really that many people with something worth saying?"
  - More recent and still controversial: Facebook and Twitter.
- He knowingly groups "truly bad" and "seemed bad but turned out very good" together because they can't be told apart beforehand.
- His core claim: "The best product ideas are often found in the 'bad ideas' category!"

chunks.heading: Why category 3 is the "low hanging fruit"
chunks.text:
- Outside the super-genius research case and the cost-collapse case, he says the real low-hanging fruit is likely in the "bad ideas" category.
- The price is dealing with "annoying skeptics and haters" who say you're wasting your time.
- The payoff is that sometimes you create something hugely important, or at least moderately successful, and the skeptics don't.

chunks.heading: Experts are bad at picking winners (the Google Video lesson)
chunks.text:
- He says everyone thinks they can tell the good ideas, but observation suggests they can't.
- Some people are better at picking winners than others, but "at best they have maybe 50% accuracy". He has seen very smart people, including at Google, be very wrong.
- Example: when "upload videos and put them on the web" Google Video was first developed, nearly everyone at Google, including Paul, was skeptical that anything worthwhile would be uploaded. The common prediction was "movies and porn."
- The skeptics were completely wrong about the lack of worthwhile content. He calls uploaded video "one of the most important developments of the past several years."
- Google Video had an "incredibly bad upload process" (it required installing a Windows client). YouTube, started after Google Video launched, took over.
- He believes that mistake was partly caused by the negative expectations around the idea.

chunks.heading: Test ideas instead of debating them
chunks.text:
- Lesson: "Instead of endlessly debating whether an idea is good or not, we should find faster and cheaper ways of testing them."
- This is why open systems like the Internet or market economies develop faster than closed systems like communism or big companies: individuals and small groups can build new things without anyone's approval.

chunks.heading: Your idea is worth little until you build it
chunks.text:
- Lesson: "Your product idea is generally worthless, because to most people it's indistinguishable [from] other bad ideas."
- Very few people will buy, steal or take your idea for free, because they already have their own bad ideas they like better.
- Paul says the way to make an idea valuable is to demonstrate it's not bad by building a real product. This also demonstrates your ability to execute.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul Buchheit argues that optimization is a general process, not just CPU profiling: find the problems, rank them by benefit/cost, and fix them in that order. A small fraction of details drive most outcomes, so product builders must observe what really matters and avoid burning time on trivia.

chunks.heading: Optimization is a general discipline: find what matters, fix in ROI order
chunks.text:
Paul argues that all engineers and product designers should understand "make it better" optimization (the CS kind, not "make it optimal"). He says most people's words and behavior show they haven't internalized it. He reduces it to three steps:

1. Find the problems (profiling).
2. Sort them by benefit-of-fixing / cost-of-fixing (ROI).
3. Fix them in order, highest ROI to lowest.

He applies this to everything, not only CPU profiling. The zeroth step is deciding what you are optimizing for.

chunks.heading: Optimizing the wrong things: pennies vs. big leaks
chunks.text:
- Paul's personal-finance example: people who drive around town to save a few cents on gas, but waste thousands on a fancy car or credit card interest, put their effort into low-reward activity while losing more elsewhere.
- Big, dumb, "Dilbertesque" companies do the same: "cutting back on pencils while running super-bowl commercials."
- To optimize money, first observe where most of it comes from and where most of it goes.
- Interest rates work the same way. "What's a few percent?" on a mortgage can be one of the details that determines the outcome.

chunks.heading: Time spent on trivia is time not spent on what matters
chunks.text:
- Paul ties this to his post "Wasting time on things that really don't matter." The choice between two slightly different ways of testing for the empty string is not zero-value, but a product probably has "100,000 more serious problems."
- His rule: "fix all of the other problems first, then debate the empty string."
- The empty-string debate is only worth having if you are optimizing for endless debates or code "beauty." If you are optimizing for the success of the product, it "probably has negative value and should be strongly avoided."
- Your time is finite, so time on unimportant details is time not spent on important ones.
- Engineers are very detail-oriented. That helps when they focus on the important details and hurts when they focus on the unimportant ones. Learning to tell the difference "will be worth your time."

chunks.heading: A few details determine most of the outcome (80/20, 90/10, 99/1)
chunks.text:
- Small details still matter, because a small fraction of them decide the majority of the result. Paul calls this the 80/20 or 90/10 rule. For example, "90% of the time is spent in 10% of the code," and it could just as easily be 99/1.
- It can be a few lines in the inner loop, or the interest rate on a mortgage.
- Concrete example: at Google he profiled a server and found about 90% of the time going to a single line, a call to `sscanf` repeated millions of times, which someone had snuck into the scoring code. He calls it "the 99999/1 rule."
- Caveat he added after a commenter's pushback: 80/20 is only a heuristic. Code that has already been well optimized, such as games, HPC and embedded, tends to have flatter profiles where it may not hold.

chunks.heading: Product design: get the important details right (the iPod example)
chunks.text:
- Slashdot's 2001 summary of the newly released iPod was "No wireless. Less space than a nomad. Lame."
- By 2007 those turned out not to be the important details. There was still no wireless iPod (until the 29th of that month), and most iPods had less than the original 5GB of storage.
- Apple got a few important details right:
  - It was easy to get your music onto an iPod.
  - It held "enough" music, unlike early flash players.
  - It fit easily in a pocket, unlike early disk-based players.
- His conclusion: "If you get all of the important details right, you'll be so far ahead of everyone else that the other details probably won't matter."

chunks.heading: How to tell which details matter: observation
chunks.text:
- Paul's answer is "Observation," plus some judgment, which he thinks is mostly formed through observation.
- For an application, observe which resources are being exhausted or causing delay. It is not always CPU; it is often disk seeks. Then observe where they are consumed.
- For product design, observe which things are most useful and which are most painful or annoying. He says the pain is usually waiting or thinking.
- For money, observe where it goes and where it comes from.

chunks.heading: Raise the number of details you get right by lowering cost
chunks.text:
- The benefit/cost equation has a cost side too. Cut it so you can do more things in less time.
- His ways to cut cost: find easier solutions (he links his post "The secret to making things easy: avoid hard problems") and avoid endless debates.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul argues engineers over-focus on technically hard problems, which impress peers but rarely produce successful products. He advocates cheating technically, taking shortcuts and finding an easier route, illustrated by YouTube beating Google Video and a memcached-instead-of-database example.

chunks.heading: Avoid hard problems: the shortcut-first approach to building products
chunks.text:
Paul argues that the fastest way to make things easy is to avoid hard problems rather than solve them. In his experience most engineers prefer hard problems because they impress other engineers, but that is "not a great way to build successful products."

- His method for getting things done quickly: "cheat (technically), take a lot of shortcuts, and find an easier way around the problem."
- Guardrail: think ahead only enough to avoid painting yourself into a corner, or have a plausible plan for escaping the corner.
- "There's always an easier way -- work lazier, not harder."
- Exceptions exist, such as security and bank transactions.
- The best wins are easy solutions to important problems that look really hard. Avoiding hard problems doesn't mean avoiding things that merely seem difficult.

chunks.heading: Why YouTube beat Google Video
chunks.text:
Paul cites this as one of several reasons YouTube beat Google Video.

- Google spent a lot of time solving technically challenging problems.
- YouTube built a product people actually used, on what he believes was PHP and MySQL, "which is not at all technically impressive."
- He hedged on the stack ("I think"). In the comments he noted YouTube probably used a variety of languages as it grew, and that a "Senior web developer" job posting asked for PHP experience.

chunks.heading: Most "hard problems" are irrelevant for 99% of products
chunks.text:
Paul's example is conventional databases. Databases solve difficult problems, and people rightly warn against reinventing the wheel. But many of those problems don't apply to most products.

- "Real" databases can handle transactions too large to fit in memory. That mattered in 1980.
- In 2007 a computer with 32GB of memory cost around $5,000.
- His guess for Twitter: transactions of roughly 0.0000002 GB (messages capped at 140 characters), not gigabyte-sized ones.
- Takeaway: check whether the hard problem a tool solves is one you actually have.

chunks.heading: Don't ditch what works: understand, then fix
chunks.text:
Paul is explicit that he is not telling people to abandon their database.

- If the database is plenty fast, "the easiest thing to do is probably 'nothing', and that's what I advise you do."
- If it's slow or overloaded, do two things: 1. understand the problem, 2. fix the problem.
- The right fix depends on the situation.

chunks.heading: Split data by how much correctness it needs
chunks.text:
When a database is overloaded, Paul suggests separating data by importance.

- Important data that rarely changes (username and password): leave it in the database.
- Data that updates constantly and doesn't need to be exactly correct (last active time, hit counters): move it into something "really simple but less reliable."

His example of simple but less reliable:
1. All updates go into memcached, but not the database.
2. (Optional) A background process occasionally copies entries from memcached to the database. Without this, the values are completely lost when memcached restarts.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Paul tells how he drifted into Silicon Valley with no plan, sent resumes to technically interesting startups, and ended up at Google despite doubting it would win. His lesson: you don't need it all figured out, so keep moving, seek uncertain opportunities, and treat early startup jobs as education.

chunks.heading: Learning by moving: "You don't need to have it all figured out right now"
chunks.text:
Paul has always wanted to start an important company or build something everyone will use. In college (Ohio) he got interested in founding or joining a software startup but had no idea how to do either. His only plan was to move to Silicon Valley, since that's where the cool startups seemed to be.

- He joined Intel in Santa Clara in 1998, after a friend (Chad) took a job there.
- His core advice: "You don't need to have it all figured out right now. The important thing is to keep moving forward."
- He urges seeking "opportunities to learn or try something new, something with uncertain outcomes."

chunks.heading: Finding a startup with almost no research
chunks.text:
After almost a year in Intel's cubicles ("two shades of gray"), Paul wanted something new. He didn't know much about startups, and the ones in "Red Herring" magazine all sounded boring.

- He skipped intelligent research. He read Slashdot at Intel and sent his resume to the handful of local startups that sounded technically interesting.
- Most never replied. One offered him a job: Google.
- At the time Google was a small team in a little office on University Ave in Palo Alto.
- What drew him: he liked the product, the people seemed smart, the work sounded interesting, and the office felt bright and high energy.

chunks.heading: Joining Google while doubting it would win
chunks.text:
Paul says Google's "business model" seemed pretty unlikely to him, and he assumed it probably wouldn't make it.

- His reasoning: Altavista had more users, money, engineers, and "more everything." If Google took off, Altavista could simply match the product and kill it.
- He took the job anyway as "a fun job and a great opportunity to meet new people and learn more about startups," planning to find a better startup next time.
- He was "only half-right": the "Altavista crushes Google" outcome never happened, but Google was a great opportunity to meet people and learn about startups, technology, and products.
- Takeaway: his predictions about which startup would win were wrong, so the choice was driven by learning and people, not a confident forecast.

chunks.heading: Advice: go join a startup, treat it as education
chunks.text:
If you're interested in startups, Paul says don't wait for the perfect opportunity. Find one that sounds interesting and get a job there.

- "The startup will probably fail, but you will succeed because you have learned a lot more than you otherwise would have."
- Big companies teach things too, but he jokes that you can learn "how to be a worker bee."
- Seek uncertain outcomes on purpose; the learning is the payoff, not the startup's survival.

chunks.heading: Defending "just find one that sounds interesting" against the "right thing" objection
chunks.text:
A commenter (Nivi) argued people should focus on doing the "right things" rather than doing things right, and warned against joining companies casually. Paul's reply:

- The future is very difficult to predict. In 1999 many people thought the world didn't need another search engine and that Google was the "wrong thing."
- If there's a business you really believe in, join that.
- Otherwise, "look at it more as a learning experience, a part of your education, and find someplace where you can learn a lot."

chunks.heading: Leaving a comfortable job for uncertainty
chunks.text:
Paul quit Google in 2006 because "life at Google had become too predictable, and too typical." He chose to move toward "something new, something uncertain."

- The same principle applies at every stage: when a role stops stretching you, leave and take on something with an uncertain outcome.

Experimentation and testing always beats speculation and debate. Rapid experimentation and iteration produces rapid learning and progress. This is one reason why it is possible for startups to beat much larger companies (Spacex provides another great example of this principle)

Fewer than 0.1% of startups will ever be worth more than $100B, but those that do will have an outsized impact, so it’s worth understanding which companies have the potential and what it takes to get there.

Examining the history of these massively successful companies, it becomes clear that there are two ingredients necessary to reach $100B.

First, they must be building in a rapidly growing market of unlimited size. For example, Microsoft, Apple, Intel and AMD all emerged as part of the exponentially growing microcomputer market. These companies started when microcomputers were still relatively new and obscure. Micro-soft’s first product, Altair BASIC, was incredibly niche — MITS only ever sold about 25,000 Altairs, but that was the start of what is now a $3T company.

Likewise, Amazon, Google, and Facebook all became $T companies by growing with the Internet. Stripe ($160B) makes this dynamic explicit in its mission statement: “Our mission is to increase the GDP of the internet”.

Why now? $100B opportunities only exist for a limited time. If a company could have been started 20 years earlier, then it’s unlikely to have $100B potential. Important new technologies create massive new opportunities, but those windows of opportunity don’t last forever. For example, it was not possible to start Uber or DoorDash five years earlier because mobile platforms such as the iPhone did not yet exist, and it wasn’t possible to create them five years later because the opportunity had already been captured.

Large but slow growing markets rarely produce $100B companies. For example, startups selling to dentists or auto mechanics are not good candidates to reach $100B. A simple test is to ask if demand will increase 10x or 100x in the next ten years. Startups thrive when capturing a slice of a rapidly growing pie, not fighting zero-sum games against incumbents.

The second ingredient is defensibility, a durable control point in the market. If your company is making billions of dollars, that will attract a lot of interest from potential competitors.

This defensibility is typically provided by one or more of the following dynamics:

- Marketplaces like Amazon, Google, Facebook, and Uber aggregate supply and demand.

- Platforms like Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Salesforce, and OpenAI provide a foundation for large ecosystems to grow.

- Foundational infrastructure companies like TSMC, AWS, Stripe, and Arm become hard-to-replace dependencies.

- Workflow systems like ServiceNow, Intuit, SAP, Oracle, and Workday become the default systems of record and action.

- Deep tech companies like ASML, Tesla, and SpaceX require extraordinary technical, manufacturing, operational, regulatory, and capital execution to reproduce.

Competing head-on with these companies is nearly impossible. They effectively “own” their slice of a large and rapidly growing market, which earns them high revenue multiples, lower cost of capital, and the ability to acquire smaller companies and hire top talent.

Probably fewer than 1% of startups have the potential to reach $100B, and of those, fewer than 10% will ever realize that potential. However, it is our belief that we can improve those odds by building a community of the most impressive founders working on the most ambitious ideas.
